1Databricks + Lakehouse ArchitectureQ1-8

Q1Untaggeddesign

Explain the control plane vs. compute plane split. Where do your data, your compute, and your metadata physically live in classic compute vs. serverless? What changes for networking, security, and cost when you move a workload to serverless?

My original note

Control Plane manages Databricks; Compute Plane runs my workload. Classic compute gives me more infrastructure control, while serverless shifts more infrastructure management to Databricks.

text
PySpark code
 ↓
Spark job
 ↓
Driver
 ↓
Executors
 ↓
Actual processing

Classic More infrastructure control → more networking/configuration responsibility

Tumhe cluster configuration, networking model, access, policies etc. ke around zyada control mil sakta hai.

Serverless More Databricks-managed infrastructure → less infrastructure management

Benefit:

  • faster provisioning
  • less cluster-management overhead
  • easier operational experience
  • consumption-oriented cost model can be attractive for suitable workloads

But trade-off: You give up some low-level infrastructure control in exchange for simplicity.

Expanded answer

I split Databricks into two parts. The control plane is the brain. The compute plane is the muscle.

Control plane. Databricks runs it in its own account. It holds the web app, the REST APIs, cluster and job management, and login and access checks. Databricks describes it as the backend services in the Databricks account, not my cloud account.

Compute plane. This is where my data is processed. There are two kinds:

Classic compute plane Serverless compute plane
Where the machines run My cloud account, inside my own network Databricks account, same region as my workspace
Who sets up the network Me Databricks, inside a network boundary per workspace
Who manages clusters Me (size, type, policies) Databricks
Cost shape Databricks charge plus my own cloud VM bill One usage-based bill

Where my data lives. In both cases my tables sit in cloud object storage. Compute is temporary. Storage is not. For classic workspaces, workspace storage buckets sit in my cloud account. They hold notebook revisions, job results and logs.

Where metadata lives. Table definitions and permissions are governed by Unity Catalog. One metastore can serve many workspaces in a region.

What changes with serverless.

  • Networking: less to build, less to tweak. I use Databricks-provided controls instead of my own network setup.
  • Security: isolation is handled by Databricks. I give up low-level knobs.
  • Cost: I pay for use, and I stop paying for idle clusters. I also stop tuning VM types.

Serverless compute trades control for simplicity. That is the same trade-off written in my note.

Accuracy and gaps

Gaps in my note. The note says who manages what. It does not say where data, compute and metadata live, so I filled that in above. The PySpark flow (Driver → Executors) in this answer actually belongs to the Spark internals section, Q9.

Q2Untaggedcompare

What specific problems of the "data lake + separate warehouse" architecture does the lakehouse solve, and which of those depend on Delta Lake and Unity Catalog rather than on Databricks itself? When is a lakehouse the wrong answer?

My original note

  • Databricks → platform + compute + orchestration + workloads
  • Delta Lake → reliable transactional table/storage layer
  • Unity Catalog → centralized governance, permissions, lineage etc.

Delta Lake adds a transactional layer over Parquet. The transaction log provides ACID semantics, consistent snapshots, concurrency control, and reliable table versions, which plain Parquet as a file format does not provide by itself.

Expanded answer

The old problem. Teams kept raw files in a lake and copied cleaned data into a warehouse. That meant two copies, two sets of permissions, and a copy job that could break.

What the lakehouse changes. I keep one copy of data in object storage. I put a table layer on top. I query it with SQL, Python or ML tools.

Who does what.

Problem Fixed by
Half-written files, no safe updates Delta Lake (transaction log)
Many copies of permissions Unity Catalog
Running jobs, clusters, SQL The Databricks platform

So three of the benefits belong to open pieces or governance pieces. They are not magic from the platform alone. Delta Lake is open source, and Delta ACID guarantees come from its log.

When a lakehouse is the wrong answer. My own view, added by me:

  • Very high rate of tiny single-row writes with millisecond reads. That is an OLTP job. See Q8.
  • A tiny team with one small dataset. A plain database is simpler.
  • A hard rule that data must stay inside a specific database engine.

Accuracy and gaps

Gap. My note covers the "who does what" part. It does not name the specific problems or say when a lakehouse is wrong. I added both.

Q3Untaggedcompare

You have a nightly ETL, an analyst doing ad hoc exploration, and a BI dashboard with 200 concurrent users. Which compute (job compute, all-purpose cluster, SQL warehouse, serverless) would you pick for each, and why? What would make you change your mind?

My original note

Workload Natural choice Main reason
Nightly ETL Job compute Scheduled production processing
Ad-hoc analyst work Interactive/all-purpose Interactive exploration
200-user BI SQL Warehouse SQL + concurrency
Serverless Deployment/management option Less infrastructure management

Expanded answer

My picks match the table. I add the "what would change my mind" part.

  • Nightly ETL → job compute. It starts, runs, and shuts down. I do not pay for idle time.
  • I would change to serverless jobs if I do not want to manage clusters or tune start-up.
  • I would change to a SQL warehouse if the whole job is SQL.
  • Analyst → all-purpose cluster. It stays up for notebooks. It can be shared.
  • I would change to serverless notebooks to avoid waiting for a cluster.
  • 200 BI users → SQL warehouse. It is built for many SQL queries at once. It can add clusters when queries queue.
  • I would change my sizing if the query profile shows queueing or spill.

Serverless is not a fourth workload. It is a way to run the first three, as my note says.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. My table lists serverless as a "deployment option". That is correct. SQL warehouses also come in serverless form, so the choice is really "which engine" plus "who manages it".

Q4Untaggedconcept

How does Databricks Runtime differ from open-source Spark? What are the portability and lock-in implications of relying on Databricks-specific features?

My original note

Databricks Runtime is built around Apache Spark but adds Databricks-specific optimizations, integrations and runtime capabilities. Standard Spark code can remain portable, but relying heavily on Databricks-specific features can increase vendor lock-in and migration effort.

Expanded answer

Databricks Runtime (DBR) is Apache Spark plus extras. The extras include Photon, Delta Lake integration, Auto Loader and other Databricks features.

Portable: plain PySpark and SQL on Parquet or Delta files.

Less portable: features that only exist on Databricks. For example cloudFiles (Auto Loader), Photon-only speed-ups and Databricks-only table features.

My rule: keep business logic in standard Spark. Keep Databricks features at the edges, like ingestion and scheduling.

Accuracy and gaps

Nothing missing for the question. The answer is short but correct.

Q5Untaggedconcept

What objects live at the account level vs. the workspace level? How does this affect a multi-workspace setup with shared data?

My original note

The account represents the organization-level scope, while workspaces provide separate working environments. In a multi-workspace architecture, centrally governed data and access policies can be shared across workspaces through Unity Catalog, while workspace-specific workloads and resources remain isolated.

Expanded answer

Account level is the whole organization.

  • Users, groups, service principals, SSO
  • Creating and managing workspaces
  • Unity Catalog metastores
  • Billing and usage

Workspace level is one working area.

  • Clusters and compute
  • Jobs and schedules
  • Notebooks and repos
  • Workspace settings

Databricks documents that an account holds many workspaces and metastores. I can link one metastore to many workspaces in the same region. Each workspace then sees the same data and the same access rules.

Effect on shared data: I govern data once. Teams run their own compute in their own workspace.

Q6Untaggeddesign

When do notebooks become a liability in production? How would you structure code for testing, reuse, and deployment instead?

My original note

Best for :- Explore → prototype → debug → understand data

Not good for Production :- Reusable logic → tested code → version control → deployment

Notebooks are excellent for interactive development and exploration, but they can become a liability in production when business logic, configuration and orchestration become tightly coupled. I would move reusable transformation logic into version-controlled modules, add automated tests, and use a deployment mechanism such as CI/CD and jobs to operationalize the pipeline.

text
Notebook
 │
 ├── exploration
 ├── testing ideas
 └── development
 ↓
 Python modules
 ↓
 Git
 ↓
 CI/CD
 ↓
 Lakeflow Job
 ↓
 Production

Notebook = develop/explore Modules = reusable logic Git = version control Tests = confidence Jobs/CI-CD = productionization

Expanded answer

A notebook becomes a liability when one file does everything: config, logic, and orchestration. I cannot unit test it. I cannot reuse it. Reviews are hard.

What I do instead:

  1. Put transformation logic in Python functions inside modules.
  2. Write unit tests for those functions with small DataFrames.
  3. Keep code in Git.
  4. Deploy with CI/CD. I can use Databricks Asset Bundles for that.
  5. Run it as a Lakeflow Job.

The notebook stays as a thin caller or a place to explore.

Q7Untaggedcompare

Where do open table formats and interoperability (Delta, Iceberg, UniForm) fit in current Databricks architecture? Why would a customer care?

My original note

Customers care because table-format interoperability reduces ecosystem lock-in and allows different analytical engines to work with the same underlying data. The choice becomes an architecture and interoperability decision, not just a storage-format decision.

Expanded answer

Delta and Iceberg are both Parquet data files plus a metadata layer. Parquet alone is just files.

UniForm (now called Iceberg reads on Databricks) makes Iceberg metadata next to the Delta metadata. The data files are not rewritten. One copy of data serves both Delta and Iceberg readers.

Why a customer cares: they can use other engines on the same data without copying it.

Limits I should check: the table needs column mapping, and Iceberg reads cannot be enabled on a table with deletion vectors (use REORG to purge them first). Iceberg metadata is made asynchronously, so an Iceberg reader can lag behind the latest Delta commit.

Accuracy and gaps

Version note. Docs call this feature "Iceberg reads" and say it was previously called UniForm. The newer docs also describe Iceberg v3 tables and managed Iceberg tables, which my note does not cover.

Q8Untaggeddesign

Where does an operational (OLTP-style) database fit into a lakehouse architecture today, and how does it relate to your analytical tables?

My original note

The OLTP system remains optimized for operational transactions, while the lakehouse provides a scalable analytical foundation. Data is typically replicated from the operational system through ingestion or CDC into analytical layers

Expanded answer

OLTP runs the business: many small reads and writes, fast, current data. OLAP studies the business: big reads, historical data.

The usual flow. Apps write to the OLTP database. I copy changes into the lakehouse with ingestion or CDC. I then build Bronze, Silver and Gold tables for BI and ML.

Newer option. Databricks now offers Lakebase, a managed Postgres OLTP database. It can serve lakehouse data to apps through synced tables.

Accuracy and gaps

Version note. My note says OLTP stays outside the lakehouse. That is still the common pattern. Lakebase is a newer, added option. I checked its docs but I do not know its production status for every cloud, so I would check before choosing it.

2Spark Fundamentals + InternalsQ9-26

Q9Untaggedconcept

Trace a PySpark DataFrame query from the line of code to execution on an executor. Cover the driver, logical and physical planning, the DAG, stages, tasks, and what happens when a task finishes.

My original note

The driver receives the Spark application and builds a logical plan from the DataFrame operations. Catalyst optimizes that plan and Spark creates a physical execution plan. The physical plan is represented as a DAG, which is divided into stages at shuffle boundaries. Each stage is further divided into tasks, generally one task per input partition, and those tasks are scheduled on executors where the actual data processing occurs.

Follow-up: Where does lazy evaluation matter here?

Transformations are lazy, so execution is triggered when an action is called.

Transformation = "what I want"

Action = "now actually do it"

Without cache: count() → compute

count() → compute AGAIN

With cache: count() → compute → cache

count() → reuse

Follow-up: Why does calling count() twice recompute work?

No cache → recomputation possible

Cache/persist → reuse materialized computation

Expanded answer

Step by step:

  1. I write DataFrame code. Nothing runs yet.
  2. I call an action like count() or write. Now Spark starts.
  3. The driver builds a logical plan.
  4. Catalyst cleans and optimizes it. It checks names, pushes filters down, and prunes columns.
  5. Spark picks a physical plan.
  6. The plan is cut into stages at shuffle boundaries.
  7. Each stage becomes tasks. One task per partition, usually.
  8. The driver sends tasks to executors. Executors read, compute and write.
  9. When a task finishes, the executor reports back to the driver. A map-side task leaves shuffle files on the executor's local disk. A final task returns or writes its result. The driver then starts the next stage.

Why count() twice does the work twice. Spark keeps the recipe, not the result. Each action reruns the recipe. cache() or persist() stores the result so later actions reuse it. See Q18 for when cache hurts.

Databricks AQE docs also note that at the end of each shuffle, exact size statistics become available. That is why AQE can change the plan while it runs.

Accuracy and gaps

Gaps and fine points. - My note does not answer "what happens when a task finishes". I added step 9. - My note says the physical plan "is represented as a DAG". More exactly, the physical plan is turned into an RDD graph, and the scheduler cuts that graph into stages. The idea is the same.

Q10Untaggedconcept

Given a query with a filter, groupBy, join, distinct, window, and orderBy, which operations cause a shuffle, which don't, and where do the stage boundaries fall? What exactly happens to data when Spark hits a shuffle?

My original note

Shuffle = redistribute data from one partition/execution to another partition/execution.

Expensive bcuz it can involve:- network I/O + disk I/O + serialization + sorting + memory pressure

groupBy() — Shuffle

python
df.groupBy("customer_id").sum("amount")
text
P1: C1 C2 C3
P2: C2 C4 C1
P3: C3 C1 C4

Spark needs:-
C1 → all together
C2 → all together
C3 → all together
C4 → all together

Stage 1
P1 ──┐
P2 ──┼──► SHUFFLE ──► Stage 2
P3 ──┘

join() - shuffle

text
Orders ─────┐
            ├──► SHUFFLE BY customer_id ──► JOIN
Customers ──┘

A normal join often requires shuffle based on the join key, but broadcast join can avoid shuffling the large side.

distinct() — Shuffle

text
P1 → C1 C2
P2 → C2 C3
P3 → C1 C3

C1 exists both in P1 & P3 -> so needs to be deduplicated based on both partitions not just locally, hence moving similar records into one partition is useful here based on customer_id key

text
P1 ──┐
P2 ──┼──► SHUFFLE ──► Deduplicate
P3 ──┘

orderBy() - shuffle

Global orderBy() is a shuffle-heavy operation.

text
orderBy()
 ↓
Global redistribution + sorting
 ↓
Expensive
Operation Shuffle? Why?
filter() Usually No Existing partitions can be filtered independently
groupBy() Yes Need to collect data based on same keys
join() Usually Yes Has to move matching keys to a same place
distinct() Yes Duplicate values identification
window() Often Yes Partitioning + ordering required
orderBy() Yes Global ordering

Shuffle boundary:-

python
result = (
   sales
   .filter("amount > 1000")
   .groupBy("customer_id")
   .sum("amount")
   .orderBy("sum(amount)")
)

Expanded answer

What happens at a shuffle. Every map task splits its output by key and writes it to local shuffle files. Reduce tasks in the next stage fetch their pieces over the network. Rows with the same key end up in the same partition.

Why it hurts. Network, disk, serialization, sorting and memory all get used. This matches my note.

In my example query:

  • filter has no shuffle. It runs inside Stage 1.
  • groupBy shuffles. Stage 1 ends and Stage 2 begins.
  • orderBy shuffles again. Stage 3 sorts.

Window functions. With PARTITION BY, Spark shuffles by that key. With no PARTITION BY, all rows go to one partition. That is a classic slowdown. This is my added knowledge.

Join. A broadcast join avoids shuffling the big side. I cover it in Q13.

Accuracy and gaps

Fine points. - Spark usually does a partial aggregation before the groupBy shuffle, so less data moves. My note shows raw rows moving for simplicity. - The AQE feature in Databricks may change the number of post-shuffle partitions at run time. See Q15.

Q11Untaggedtroubleshooting

A pipeline got slower after someone added repartition(200). Give at least four reasons this can happen. Then explain when repartition vs. coalesce is the right choice, and what you'd lose by picking the wrong one.

My original note

Partition is a chunk of data which is processed by spark using tasks.

If the data is really large, then creating more partitions can definitely improve the parallel processing.

But in case of small data, more partitions can simply add to

Expanded answer

A partition is a chunk of data. One task works on one partition.

Reasons repartition(200) can slow a job:

  1. It adds a full shuffle. All data moves over the network.
  2. Too many tiny tasks on small data. Task start-up costs more than the work.
  3. It can undo a good layout. Data that was already well split gets reshuffled.
  4. More small output files when writing. That hurts later reads.
  5. Fixed 200 ignores the data. It may be too few for big data and too many for small data.

repartition vs coalesce:

repartition(n) coalesce(n)
Shuffle Yes, full No (merges partitions)
Can increase partitions Yes No
Even sizes Yes Not guaranteed
Use when I need more parallelism or balanced data I need fewer partitions, for example before a write

If I pick wrong: using repartition to reduce wastes a shuffle. Using coalesce to cut too hard can leave a few big partitions and lose parallelism.

Accuracy and gaps

Incomplete in my note. The last sentence stops mid-way: "more partitions can simply add to". It most likely meant "add to overhead". Also, "definitely improve" is too strong. More partitions help only if there is enough data and enough cores. I flagged this as a correction, not a silent change.

Q12Untaggedtroubleshooting

In the Spark UI, one task in a stage runs 50x longer than the others. How do you determine whether it's skew, a bad node, spill, a big partition, or GC? What evidence distinguishes them?

Expanded answer

I open the stage page and sort tasks by duration. Then I compare the slow task with the median task.

Cause Evidence I look for
Skew Shuffle read size or records is much larger than the median. Many tasks are fine.
Big input partition Input size is large for that task. Often one huge unsplittable file.
Spill "Spill (memory)" and "Spill (disk)" columns are non-zero for that task.
GC GC time is a big part of the task time. Memory is tight.
Bad node Input size is normal, but the task is slow. Other tasks on the same host are slow too. It may run fine on retry.

First question I ask: is the slow task also the biggest task? If yes, think data (skew, big partition). If no, think machine (bad node, GC, spill).

Q13Untaggedconcept

Walk through what happens physically during a broadcast join. When can a broadcast join make performance worse or fail outright? How do the broadcast threshold, hints, and AQE interact?

Expanded answer

What happens.

  1. Spark collects the small table to the driver.
  2. The driver sends a copy to every executor.
  3. Each executor builds a hash table of it.
  4. Each task joins its own big-table partition against that hash table.

The big table is never shuffled.

When it hurts or fails.

  • The "small" table is not small. The driver or executors run out of memory.
  • Collecting and sending takes too long, or a broadcast timeout hits.
  • Join type limits. For example, the left side of a left outer join cannot be broadcast.
  • Bad size estimates. Spark thinks a table is small, but it is not.

How threshold, hints and AQE fit together.

  • The static threshold lets the planner pick a broadcast join when it estimates the table is small.
  • A hint like BROADCAST tells Spark to do it anyway.
  • AQE can switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join at run time using real sizes. The Databricks default threshold for this switch is 30 MB.
  • The docs say a join planned as broadcast from the start is usually faster than one switched by AQE. AQE may switch only after both sides were already shuffled.
Q14Untaggedcompare

You have three valid join strategies: broadcast hash, shuffle hash, and sort-merge. How does Spark choose between them, when would you override it, and what could go wrong?

Expanded answer

Strategy How it works Good when
Broadcast hash Copy small side to all executors One side is small
Shuffle hash Shuffle both sides, build a hash table per partition Build side is moderate and fits in memory
Sort-merge Shuffle and sort both sides, then merge Both sides are large. Safe default

How Spark chooses. It looks at hints first. Then join type and size estimates. Small enough side → broadcast. Otherwise, sort-merge is the usual default.

When I override. I use a hint (BROADCAST, SHUFFLE_HASH, MERGE) when I know the data better than the statistics do.

What can go wrong.

  • Stale statistics make a bad choice.
  • A forced broadcast of a big table causes out-of-memory.
  • Shuffle hash with a big build side runs out of memory.
  • A hint can become wrong as data grows.

On Databricks, Photon replaces sort-merge joins with its own hash joins for supported queries.

Q15Untaggedconcept

What does AQE actually do at runtime, and why does it need shuffle statistics to do it? Which problems does it solve, and which can it not solve (e.g. a skewed aggregation)?

Expanded answer

AQE (adaptive query execution) re-plans the query while it runs. The reason is simple. Before the run, Spark only has estimates. After a shuffle, it has the real sizes. Databricks says it has accurate statistics at the end of each shuffle or broadcast stage.

What AQE does:

  1. Switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast join when a side turns out small.
  2. Coalesces many small shuffle partitions into fewer bigger ones.
  3. Splits skewed partitions in a join.
  4. Removes work for empty relations.

What it cannot solve.

  • A skewed aggregation (groupBy on a hot key). AQE's skew handling is for joins.
  • Streaming queries. AQE applies to non-streaming queries.
  • Bad queries, such as an accidental cross join.
  • Skew that is below its detection thresholds.

AQE needs the shuffle to finish first. It only fixes what comes after a shuffle.

Q16Untaggedtroubleshooting

How would you read an explain(formatted) plan to confirm that predicate pushdown and column pruning are happening? Describe the phases of Catalyst that produced it.

Expanded answer

Reading the plan. I find the scan node at the bottom.

  • Predicate pushdown: the filter shows up in the scan's pushed filters, not only in a separate Filter node above.
  • Column pruning: the scan's read schema lists only the columns I need.
  • Partition pruning: partition filters are listed on the scan.

If the filter is only above the scan, the pushdown did not happen.

Catalyst phases.

  1. Analysis. Resolve column and table names.
  2. Logical optimization. Push filters down, prune columns, fold constants.
  3. Physical planning. Choose join and scan strategies.
  4. Code generation. Fuse operators into compact code.

My original diagram shows the same chain: Unresolved Logical Plan → Analyzed → withCachedData → Optimized → Physical → Executable → RDD.

Q17Untaggedconcept

What do Tungsten and whole-stage code generation do, and why do Python UDFs break the benefit?

Expanded answer

Tungsten makes Spark use memory and CPU better. It stores rows in a compact binary form and avoids many Java objects.

Whole-stage code generation fuses several operators, such as filter and project, into one tight function. This avoids calling one operator after another per row.

Why Python UDFs break it. A Python UDF runs in a separate Python process. Rows must be serialized, sent to Python, run row by row, and sent back. Spark cannot fuse the UDF into generated code. Photon does not support UDFs either, so that part falls back to the Spark runtime.

My fixes: use built-in functions first. If I need Python, use pandas UDFs (see Q24 and Q30).

Q18Untaggedcompare

When can caching make a workload slower or even cause failures? Compare cache vs. persist storage levels, and explain how Spark caching differs from the Databricks disk cache.

Expanded answer

When caching hurts.

  • I use the data only once. The cache costs time and gives nothing back.
  • The cached data is bigger than memory. It evicts other useful data or spills.
  • Memory pressure leads to GC pauses or out-of-memory.
  • The cache goes stale if the source changes.

cache vs persist. cache() is persist() with a default storage level. persist() lets me pick the level, such as memory only, memory and disk, or serialized forms.

Spark cache vs Databricks disk cache.

Spark cache Disk cache
What it stores A computed DataFrame Copies of remote data files
Where Executor memory (and disk) Local SSD on workers
I control it with cache() / persist() Cluster setting
Risk Memory pressure, stale data Stale view is less likely since it caches files

Accuracy and gaps

Note. I did not find a documentation page for the disk-cache details that I could verify, so I left it unlinked. I list it under "Documentation links to verify" in the validation report.

Q19Untaggedconcept

Explain the Spark unified memory model. Why might an executor OOM when the data "should fit" in memory? How does that differ from a driver OOM?

Expanded answer

Unified memory. Executor memory has one shared pool. Execution (joins, sorts, aggregations, shuffles) and storage (cached data) share it. Execution can borrow space from storage, up to a limit.

Why an executor runs out when data "should fit":

  • Rows in memory are bigger than rows on disk. Objects have overhead.
  • A single partition is far larger than average (skew).
  • Joins and aggregations build big hash tables.
  • Python and native work use memory outside the JVM heap.
  • Many tasks run at once on one executor, each taking a share.

Driver OOM is different. It happens when too much lands on the driver: collect(), toPandas(), a large broadcast, or huge file listings.

Executor OOM Driver OOM
Usual cause Big partitions, skew, wide operations Collecting data, broadcast, too many files
Fix Smaller partitions, fix skew, more memory per task Do not collect, avoid large broadcast
Q20Untaggedtroubleshooting

What is spill, why does it happen, how do you detect it, and when is spill acceptable vs. a red flag?

Expanded answer

Spill means Spark writes data from memory to disk because an operation needs more memory than it has. It happens in sorts, joins and aggregations.

Detect. In the Spark UI stage page, I check the "Spill (memory)" and "Spill (disk)" metrics.

Acceptable: small amounts. The job still finishes and time is fine.

Red flag:

  • Spill is large compared to the data size.
  • It appears on slow tasks.
  • It repeats on every run and grows over time.

Fixes: more partitions (smaller chunks), fix skew, more memory per task, fewer concurrent tasks per executor.

Q21Untaggedconcept

Walk through Spark's fault tolerance: what happens on task failure, executor loss, shuffle file loss, and driver loss? What role does lineage play, and what does speculation add?

Expanded answer

Failure What happens
Task fails The scheduler retries it, up to a limit.
Executor lost Its running tasks are rescheduled. Its shuffle output is lost too, so lost work may be recomputed.
Shuffle file lost A reducer gets a fetch failure. Spark reruns the map tasks that wrote the missing files.
Driver lost The application fails. A job retry or a restart is needed. Streaming resumes from its checkpoint.

Lineage is the recipe of how each partition was made. Spark uses it to recompute only what was lost.

Speculation launches a second copy of a slow task. The first copy to finish wins. It helps with slow nodes. It does not help with skew, because the copy gets the same big data.

Q22Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: A bug "only appears" when a particular action runs, and non-deterministic functions (e.g. rand(), uuid()) give different results across recomputations. Explain why, and how you'd protect against it.

Expanded answer

Why. Spark is lazy. Each action may recompute the DataFrame from the start. rand() and uuid() run again each time, so values change. A bug can "appear" only when one action recomputes a path that another did not.

How I protect against it.

  • Materialize once. Write the result to a table and read it back.
  • Use cache() only as a helper. A cache can be evicted and recomputed.
  • Create IDs from stable data, for example a hash of business keys.
  • If I need random numbers, set a seed. Even then, results can change if partitioning changes.
  • Keep non-deterministic steps out of retried or recomputed paths.
Q23Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: How do you decide the number of shuffle partitions and input partition sizes for a 2 TB job? What breaks if the number is too low or too high, and how does AQE change the answer?

Expanded answer

Rule of thumb (mine, not from docs): aim for about 100–200 MB per partition.

  • 2 TB ≈ 2,000,000 MB. At 200 MB each, that is about 10,000 partitions.
  • For input, Spark's file reading targets roughly 128 MB per partition by default.

Too low: big partitions, spill, out-of-memory, slow tasks, poor use of cores.

Too high: many tiny tasks, high scheduling overhead, many small output files.

With AQE. The shuffle partition setting defaults to 200, and AQE can coalesce small post-shuffle partitions. So I can set the count a bit high and let AQE shrink it. AQE does not split big partitions in an aggregation, so I still must not set it too low.

Q24Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Where does serialization cost show up in Spark (shuffle, caching, Python↔JVM)? How do Arrow and pandas UDFs change that?

Expanded answer

Serialization turns objects into bytes so they can move or be stored.

  • Shuffle: rows are serialized to write and read shuffle files.
  • Caching: serialized cache levels trade memory for CPU.
  • Python ↔ JVM: every row crossing to Python and back is serialized. This is the costly one.

Arrow and pandas UDFs. Arrow moves data in columnar batches instead of row by row. A pandas UDF works on a whole batch (a pandas Series) at once. That cuts per-row overhead a lot. It is still slower than a built-in function.

Q25Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Why does the narrow vs. wide dependency distinction matter for both performance and recovery cost?

Expanded answer

Narrow: each output partition depends on one input partition. Examples: filter, select. No shuffle. Fast. If a partition is lost, I recompute just that one.

Wide: each output partition depends on many input partitions. Examples: groupBy, join. Needs a shuffle. Slower. If output is lost, I may need to rebuild from many parent partitions.

So wide dependencies cost more at run time, and cost more to recover. They also mark the stage boundaries.

Q26Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: A join key has a few hot values. Compare salting, AQE skew-join handling, broadcasting, and isolating the hot keys. When does each fail?

Expanded answer

Fix How it works Fails when
Salting Add a random suffix to the hot key so rows spread out. Replicate the other side to match. The other side is large, so replication is costly. Code is more complex.
AQE skew join Splits skewed partitions into smaller tasks automatically Skew is not in a join, or is below the detection thresholds
Broadcast Avoids shuffling the big side Both sides are large
Isolate hot keys Handle hot keys in a separate join (often broadcast), the rest normally I do not know the hot keys, or they change often

My order of try: AQE first (it is automatic and Databricks recommends it over the hint). Then broadcast if possible. Then isolation. Then salting as the last tool.

3PySpark + SQLQ27-41

Q27Criticalcode

🔴 CRITICAL: Write PySpark to keep the latest record per business key from a table with ties on timestamp and nulls in the ordering column. Compare row_number, max(struct(...)), and dropDuplicates. Which is non-deterministic, and why?

Expanded answer

python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

w = Window.partitionBy("business_key").orderBy(
    F.col("updated_at").desc_nulls_last(),   # nulls go last
    F.col("record_id").desc()                # tie-breaker
)

latest = (df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
            .filter("rn = 1")
            .drop("rn"))
Method Behaviour
row_number() with a full tie-breaker Deterministic. One row per key.
row_number() without a tie-breaker Non-deterministic on ties. Any tied row can win.
max(struct(ts, ...)) Deterministic. Struct compares field by field, so I can build the tie-breaker into it. Nulls need care.
dropDuplicates(["key"]) Non-deterministic. It keeps an arbitrary row. It does not order anything.

Null trap. In descending order, nulls may sort first or last depending on the engine setting. I state desc_nulls_last() so the choice is explicit.

Q28Criticalcode

🔴 CRITICAL: Write SQL that collapses a CDC feed (insert/update/delete with sequence numbers, possibly out of order) into the current state per key. How would you handle deletes and the same key changing multiple times in one batch?

Expanded answer

sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY key
           ORDER BY seq DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM cdc_feed
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
  AND op <> 'D';      -- drop keys whose latest event is a delete
  • Out of order: I order by the sequence number, not by arrival time.
  • Same key many times in one batch: rn = 1 keeps only the last change.
  • Deletes: if the latest event is a delete, the key disappears from the current state. For a target table, I should apply the delete there with MERGE, not just filter it out. See Q69.
Q29Criticalcode

🔴 CRITICAL: Write SQL/PySpark for sessionization (30-minute inactivity gaps) and a running total per customer.

Follow-up: What is the default window frame, and where does ROWS vs. RANGE bite?

Follow-up: What happens to performance if one partition key is huge?

Expanded answer

Sessionization (30-minute gap).

sql
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT *,
    CASE WHEN ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)
              > INTERVAL 30 MINUTES
         OR LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) IS NULL
         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM events
)
SELECT *,
  SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS session_id
FROM gaps;

Running total per customer.

sql
SELECT customer_id, order_ts, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY order_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM orders;

Default frame. With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.

Where ROWS vs RANGE bites. RANGE includes all rows with the same order value (ties). So two orders at the same timestamp both get the same running total. ROWS counts physical rows one at a time. I use ROWS when I want a strict row-by-row total.

One huge partition key. All its rows go to one task. That task is slow and may spill or run out of memory. I fix it by splitting the key (for example by date), or by pre-aggregating.

Q30Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: Rank these from fastest to slowest for the same logic: built-in function, SQL expression, pandas UDF, Python UDF. Why? When is a UDF unavoidable, and how do you minimize the damage?

Expanded answer

Fastest to slowest:

  1. Built-in function and SQL expression (about the same, both go through Catalyst)
  2. pandas UDF (batches with Arrow)
  3. Python UDF (row by row)

Why. Built-ins can be optimized and code-generated. UDFs are black boxes. Python UDFs also pay serialization cost per row.

UDF unavoidable when the logic needs a Python library or complex custom code that built-ins cannot do.

Minimize damage:

  • Try built-in or SQL functions first.
  • Use pandas UDFs, not row UDFs.
  • Filter and prune columns before the UDF.
  • Keep the UDF small and test it.
Q31Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: List the null-handling traps in joins, filters, and aggregates: NOT IN with nulls, null join keys, count(col) vs. count(*), eqNullSafe, and null sort order. Which have caused silent wrong results?

Expanded answer

Trap What happens
NOT IN with a null in the list Returns no rows. Silent wrong result. Use NOT EXISTS or filter nulls out.
Null join keys NULL = NULL is not true, so null keys never match in a normal join. Rows can silently drop.
count(col) vs count(*) count(col) skips nulls. count(*) counts all rows.
eqNullSafe (<=>) Treats two nulls as equal. Use it when null keys should match.
Null sort order Nulls may sort first or last. Affects "latest row" logic (see Q27).

Silent wrong results: NOT IN and null join keys are the worst, since the query still succeeds.

Q32Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: A left join unexpectedly multiplies row counts in production. How do you find the cause, reconcile counts, and make the pipeline defensively reject this? Contrast left_semi/left_anti with joins in dedup/exists logic.

Expanded answer

Cause. The right side has duplicate keys. Each duplicate creates another output row.

Find it.

sql
SELECT key, COUNT(*) c FROM right_table GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Reconcile. Compare count(*) of the left table and of the join result. The difference is the extra rows.

Defend.

  • Check key uniqueness on the right side before the join. Fail the job if it is broken.
  • Deduplicate the right side explicitly (Q27).
  • Add a post-join check that output count equals left count.

semi/anti vs join. left_semi keeps left rows that have a match. It never multiplies rows. left_anti keeps left rows with no match. I use them for "exists" and "not exists" logic. A normal join for the same check can multiply rows and then need a DISTINCT.

Q33Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Explicit schema vs. inferSchema: cost, risk, and when each is acceptable. How do you handle nested structs/arrays (explode, from_json) while avoiding data loss on malformed or evolving records?

Expanded answer

inferSchema. It reads the data to guess types. Costs an extra pass over data. Types can change from run to run. Fine for quick exploration.

Explicit schema. No extra read. Stable types. Safer for production.

Nested data.

  • from_json parses a JSON string column with a schema. Bad records come back as null, so I must keep the raw string next to the parsed column.
  • explode turns array elements into rows. It drops rows with null or empty arrays. explode_outer keeps them.

Avoiding loss. Keep the raw payload. Use a rescued-data column for fields that do not fit the schema (see Q76). Do not drop unknown fields silently.

Q34Highcode

🟠 HIGH: Write PySpark that reads semi-structured input, splits valid records from bad ones, and writes bad ones to a quarantine table with enough metadata for replay. Which read modes and options do you use?

Expanded answer

python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

raw = (spark.read
  .schema(my_schema.add("_corrupt_record", "string"))
  .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
  .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record")
  .json("/Volumes/main/raw/events/")
  .withColumn("_source_file", F.col("_metadata.file_path"))
  .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp()))

raw = raw.cache()  # corrupt-record column needs a cached or saved DataFrame to filter on

good = raw.filter("_corrupt_record IS NULL").drop("_corrupt_record")
bad  = raw.filter("_corrupt_record IS NOT NULL")

good.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("main.silver.events")
bad.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("main.quarantine.events_bad")

Read modes. PERMISSIVE keeps bad rows in a corrupt-record column. DROPMALFORMED drops them. FAILFAST stops on the first bad one. I use PERMISSIVE here because I want to keep bad rows.

Metadata for replay: source file path, ingest time, the raw record, and a reason if I have one.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. The _metadata.file_path column works for file-based sources on Databricks. I did not run this code here. It is a pattern, not tested output.

Q35Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you do approximate distinct counts at scale, and when is approx_count_distinct acceptable? Why is exact COUNT(DISTINCT) expensive in Spark?

Expanded answer

Exact COUNT(DISTINCT). Spark must shuffle so equal values meet, then dedupe. That needs memory and network.

approx_count_distinct. It uses a sketch (HyperLogLog). It is much cheaper. It returns a close estimate with a small error.

Acceptable for: dashboards, trends, rough sizing. Not acceptable for: billing, audits, reconciliation. There I need the exact number.

Q36Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: Given a slow SQL query with a correlated subquery and SELECT DISTINCT, how do you rewrite and validate it? What would you read in the plan?

Expanded answer

Rewrite ideas.

  • Replace a correlated subquery with a join, or with EXISTS / left_semi.
  • Pre-aggregate in a CTE, then join.
  • Remove DISTINCT if a semi join already guarantees unique rows.

Validate.

  1. Compare row counts and a checksum of both results.
  2. Compare EXPLAIN plans.
  3. Compare run time on the same data, with a warm cache each time.

In the plan I look for: a nested-loop or repeated subquery execution, extra shuffle for DISTINCT, and whether filters are pushed to the scan.

Q37Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Pivot/unpivot on high-cardinality columns: what goes wrong at scale and what do you do instead?

Expanded answer

What goes wrong. A pivot creates one column per distinct value. With high cardinality that means thousands of columns. Spark has to find the distinct values first (an extra job). Tables get wide and slow. Memory use grows.

Instead.

  • Keep data in a long format (key, name, value).
  • Pivot only a fixed, small list of values.
  • Use maps or arrays for flexible attributes.
  • Do the reshape in the BI layer if it is only for display.
Q38Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Why does a loop of withColumn calls slow planning? What are the dangers of collect() and toPandas() in pipeline code?

Expanded answer

withColumn in a loop. Each call adds a new projection to the plan. Hundreds of them make the plan deep. Analysis and optimization get slow. I use one select with all expressions instead.

collect() and toPandas(). They pull all rows to the driver. The driver can run out of memory. It also breaks parallelism, since work becomes single-machine. I use them only on small results.

Q39Criticalcode

🔴 CRITICAL: Implement an incremental load driven by a high-water mark. Which bugs can silently lose or duplicate rows (timestamp ties, late-committing transactions, clock skew, timezone), and how do you guard against each?

Expanded answer

python
last = spark.sql("SELECT max_ts FROM ctl.watermarks WHERE src='orders'").first()[0]

new = (spark.read.table("src.orders")
         .filter(F.col("updated_at") > F.lit(last) - F.expr("INTERVAL 10 MINUTES")))  # lookback

from delta.tables import DeltaTable

(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t")
   .merge(new.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
   .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())

# save the new high-water mark only AFTER the merge succeeds
Bug Guard
Timestamp ties (> skips rows equal to the mark) Use >= plus an idempotent MERGE, or a lookback
Late-committing transactions (row commits after I read past it) Lookback window
Clock skew between systems Use the source's own commit time or a sequence column
Timezone mismatch Store everything in UTC
Saving mark before success Save the mark only after the write succeeds

Because of the lookback, the same rows can come twice. MERGE on a key makes that safe.

Q40Mediumcode

🟡 MEDIUM: Write analytical SQL for month-over-month growth, top-N per group, and a retention cohort. How would you validate the output at scale?

Expanded answer

sql
-- Month-over-month growth
WITH m AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_ts) AS month, SUM(amount) AS rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1)
SELECT month, rev,
       (rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS mom_growth
FROM m;

-- Top 3 products per category
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT category, product, SUM(amount) AS rev,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) AS rn
  FROM sales GROUP BY category, product)
WHERE rn <= 3;

-- Retention cohort
WITH first AS (SELECT user_id, date_trunc('month', MIN(ts)) AS cohort FROM events GROUP BY 1),
act AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, date_trunc('month', ts) AS active_month FROM events)
SELECT f.cohort, months_between(a.active_month, f.cohort) AS month_n,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS users
FROM first f JOIN act a USING (user_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2;

Validate at scale. Check totals against the source. Spot-check a few groups by hand. Check that month 0 of each cohort equals cohort size. Compare to a sample computed independently.

Q41Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Is a CTE materialized or re-evaluated each time it's referenced? Describe a case where a multiply-referenced CTE is silently expensive.

Expanded answer

In Spark SQL, a CTE is mostly a name for a query. It is generally re-evaluated each time it is referenced. The optimizer may reuse some work, but I should not count on it.

Silent cost example. A CTE does a big join and aggregation. Then the main query references it three times (for a self-join, for a total and for a rank). The big work may run three times.

Fix. Write the CTE result to a temp table or cache it, then reference that. I then check the plan for repeated scans.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. I wrote this from general Spark knowledge. I did not find a Databricks doc page that states this precisely, so the CTE behaviour may vary by engine version. The way to be sure is to read the query plan.

4Delta Lake + InternalsQ42-59

Q42Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: What is stored in _delta_log, and how does a reader reconstruct a consistent snapshot? Explain commits, actions (add/remove/metadata/protocol), and the role of checkpoints.

Follow-up: What happens when a transaction commits?

Expanded answer

_delta_log is a folder next to the data files. It holds the table's history.

  • Commit files. One JSON file per version (000...0.json, 000...1.json, and so on). Each lists actions.
  • Checkpoint files. Parquet files that save the full table state at some version.

Actions I should know:

Action Meaning
metaData Schema, partitioning, table settings
protocol Minimum reader and writer versions
add A data file is now part of the table
remove A data file is no longer part of the table
commitInfo Who did what, and when

How a reader builds a snapshot.

  1. Find the latest checkpoint.
  2. Read the commit files after it.
  3. Replay add and remove actions in order.
  4. The files left standing are the table at that version.

What happens when a transaction commits. First, data files are written. Then one new commit file is written to the log. Databricks explains that the log controls commit atomicity. Data files are not part of the table until the log records a new version. A failed write leaves stray files that no reader sees.

Q43Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Two jobs modify the same Delta table at the same time. Explain optimistic concurrency control, how conflicts are detected, isolation levels, and row-level concurrency. Which operation combinations conflict (blind append, UPDATE, MERGE, OPTIMIZE) and how do you design around them?

Expanded answer

Optimistic concurrency control (OCC). There are no locks. Each writer goes through three steps, as Databricks describes:

  1. Read the latest table version if needed.
  2. Write new data files.
  3. Validate and commit. Check whether another commit changed things I read or touched. If not, commit. If yes, the write fails with a concurrent modification error.

Isolation levels. By default, Databricks uses write serializable for writes and snapshot isolation for reads. Reads never block.

Row-level concurrency. With deletion vectors or liquid clustering enabled, two writers can change different rows in the same file without conflict. Without it, they conflict if they touch the same files.

Which combinations can conflict (general pattern):

Pair Conflict?
Append + append No
Append + OPTIMIZE No
UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE + same Yes, if they touch the same files (rows, with row-level concurrency)
OPTIMIZE + UPDATE / DELETE / MERGE Can conflict, unless row-level concurrency is on

Design around it. Keep writers on disjoint partitions or key ranges. Use liquid clustering or deletion vectors. Retry on conflict. Keep OPTIMIZE out of the heaviest write windows.

Accuracy and gaps

Version note. Older doc pages say Delta supports transactions per table only. Newer pages describe multi-statement and multi-table transactions with BEGIN ATOMIC on tables with catalog commits. This depends on version and feature status, so I check the current transaction docs before I rely on it. I did not verify the full conflict matrix against the docs page, so I treat my table as a pattern.

Q44Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: What happens internally during a Delta MERGE, step by step? Why is it expensive, and how do partition/clustering layout, file size, deletion vectors, and Photon influence cost?

Follow-up: How do you identify the bottleneck?

Follow-up: What if the target is several terabytes?

Follow-up: How do you make it rerunnable, and what if two jobs execute concurrently?

Expanded answer

Steps inside a MERGE.

  1. Find touched files. Join source to target on the ON condition to find which target files have matches.
  2. Rewrite. Rewrite those files with updates, deletes and inserts applied.
  3. Commit. Add the new files and remove the old ones in one log commit.

Why it is expensive. It runs joins (shuffles). And it rewrites whole files, even to change one row.

What changes the cost:

  • Layout. If target data is clustered or partitioned by the merge key, fewer files are touched. Liquid clustering helps here.
  • File size. Very big files mean big rewrites. Very small files mean many tasks.
  • Deletion vectors. They mark rows changed without rewriting the whole Parquet file.
  • Photon. It speeds up joins and writes, and uses deletion vectors for predictive I/O updates.

Find the bottleneck. I check table history for merge metrics (scan time vs rewrite time), then the Spark UI for shuffle, skew and spill.

Several-TB target. Add a partition or cluster predicate in the ON clause. Enable deletion vectors. Merge smaller batches. Make sure the source is deduplicated.

Rerunnable. Make the merge idempotent: dedupe the source and match on a key. Add a sequence check so an old row never overwrites a new one.

Two jobs at once. They can conflict (Q43). I keep them on disjoint key ranges, enable row-level concurrency, and retry.

Q45Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: What happens if the MERGE source has duplicate keys matching one target row? Describe the behavior across WHEN MATCHED clause variants (update vs. delete), and how you'd prevent or detect it upstream.

Expanded answer

UPDATE. The MERGE fails with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE. The docs explain that it is ambiguous which source row should update the target row.

DELETE. An unconditional delete is allowed with multiple matches. It is not ambiguous, since the row goes away either way.

Prevent. Deduplicate the source before the merge:

sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY seq DESC) rn FROM src)
WHERE rn = 1

Detect upstream. Run a check on the source: GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Fail the job or send those rows to quarantine.

Accuracy and gaps

Version note. The docs say that in Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS and below, MERGE only considers conditions in the ON clause before checking multiple matches. Newer runtimes also use WHEN MATCHED conditions. So the error can depend on the runtime version.

Q46Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: How does time travel work mechanically? Which retention settings control how far back you can go, and what silently breaks it?

Expanded answer

Each version of the table is a list of files in the log. Old versions stay readable as long as both the log entry and the data files still exist.

Two settings:

  • delta.logRetentionDuration: how long history is kept. Default is 30 days.
  • delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration: how long removed data files are kept before VACUUM may delete them. Default is 7 days. Databricks documents these defaults.

What silently breaks it. Running VACUUM with a short retention. Or predictive optimization running VACUUM. The log may still show version 20, but the files are gone.

So my real time-travel window is the shorter of the two settings.

Q47Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: What does VACUUM actually delete and what does it not? What can go wrong with a short retention window (long-running readers, streams, CDF consumers, time travel), and how do you pick a safe value?

Expanded answer

Deletes: data files that are no longer referenced by the table and are older than the retention window. It also removes untracked files, such as leftovers from failed writes.

Does not delete: files that the current version needs, files inside the retention window, or the log itself (the log is cleaned by its own setting).

What goes wrong with a short window:

  • A long-running query loses files it was reading.
  • A stream that is behind cannot find files for old versions.
  • A CDF consumer cannot read changes it has not processed.
  • Time travel to old versions fails.

Picking a safe value. I take the largest of: longest running query, longest stream or CDF consumer lag, and how far back I need time travel. Then I add a margin. I do not go below the 7-day default without a reason. Predictive optimization keeps a 7-day minimum.

Q48Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: What happens during OPTIMIZE? Give three or more reasons a query remains slow after OPTIMIZE, and explain how OPTIMIZE interacts with concurrent writers.

Expanded answer

What OPTIMIZE does. It rewrites many small files into fewer larger files. With clustering, it also lays out data by the clustering keys. The old files are marked removed. They stay on storage until VACUUM.

Why a query can stay slow:

  1. My filter is not on the clustering or Z-order columns, so data skipping has nothing to use.
  2. The slow part is a shuffle, skew or a join, not scanning.
  3. Statistics are not collected on the filter column.
  4. A function on the column blocks the filter.
  5. The compute is too small, or the query uses Python UDFs.
  6. New writes keep adding small files after the OPTIMIZE ran.

Concurrent writers. OPTIMIZE does not conflict with pure appends. It may conflict with UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE, unless row-level concurrency is on (Q43).

Q49Criticalcompare

🔴 CRITICAL: Compare partitioning, Z-ORDER, and liquid clustering (including automatic clustering with predictive optimization). When does partitioning hurt, how do you choose clustering keys, and what would make you change keys later?

Expanded answer

Partitioning Z-ORDER Liquid clustering
Layout Folders per value Sort-like layout across files Flexible clustering
Change keys later Rewrite the table Re-run with new columns ALTER TABLE, no rewrite of old data
Best for Low-cardinality columns, very large tables Older tables New tables

Databricks says liquid clustering replaces partitioning and Z-order for simpler layout decisions, and that it is incremental.

When partitioning hurts. High-cardinality columns create many tiny files. Skewed partitions create hot spots. Wrong partition columns cause full scans.

Choosing keys. Pick columns most used in filters. Up to 4 keys. The columns must have statistics. By default the first 32 columns have them.

Automatic clustering. CLUSTER BY AUTO on Unity Catalog managed tables lets Databricks pick keys from my query history. It changes keys only when the expected savings are more than the cost.

Changing keys later. I change them when query patterns change, or when data skipping gets poor.

Q50Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: How does data skipping work? Why might it be ineffective on a table with good filters (stats columns, column position, random distribution, file layout)?

Expanded answer

How it works. Delta stores min and max values per column for each file. When I filter, Spark skips files whose range cannot match.

Why it can fail even with good filters:

  • Stats columns. By default only the first 32 columns have stats. A filter column beyond that gets no skipping.
  • Column position. Move filter columns early in the schema, or set the stats columns explicitly.
  • Random distribution. If values are spread across all files, every file's min-max range overlaps my filter.
  • File layout. Without clustering on that column, ranges overlap.
  • Expressions. A function or cast on the column can block skipping.

Fix. Cluster by the filter columns and make sure they have statistics.

Q51Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: What produces small files in Delta (streaming, partitioned writes, frequent MERGE)? Compare optimized writes, auto compaction, and scheduled OPTIMIZE, including their tradeoffs.

Expanded answer

What makes small files. Each streaming micro-batch writes new files. A partitioned write can write one small file per partition per task. Frequent small MERGEs rewrite and add small files.

Fix When it runs Trade-off
Optimized writes During the write, adds a shuffle to build bigger files Slower writes, better files
Auto compaction After a write, a small compaction Extra work right after writes
Scheduled OPTIMIZE On my schedule Most control, but I must manage it

For Unity Catalog managed tables, predictive optimization can run OPTIMIZE for me.

Q52Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: A new column appears in the source. Walk through what happens with schema enforcement, mergeSchema, autoMerge in MERGE, and type widening. What are the dangers of turning evolution on blindly?

Expanded answer

  • Schema enforcement (default). A write with a column the table does not have is rejected.
  • mergeSchema. A write option. It adds new columns to the table schema during the write.
  • autoMerge in MERGE. A setting, or MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION, that lets a MERGE add new source columns to the target.
  • Type widening. A table feature that lets a column type grow, for example int to long, without rewriting everything.

Dangers of blind evolution.

  • Typos and junk columns pollute the table.
  • Downstream queries and BI reports can break or change.
  • Types can drift.
  • I lose the safety check that enforcement gives me.

I turn on evolution only for known sources, and I review schema changes.

Q53Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: What are deletion vectors and how do they change UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE and read behavior? When do you still need to rewrite or purge files (e.g. for GDPR)?

Expanded answer

What they are. A small side file that says "these rows in this Parquet file are deleted or changed". With deletion vectors, DELETE, UPDATE and MERGE mark rows instead of rewriting the whole file.

Effect on reads. Readers apply the deletion vector to hide marked rows. The reader must support them. Older clients cannot read the table.

When I still must rewrite or purge. The old data is still in the Parquet file. For GDPR I need to remove it physically:

  1. Run REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) to rewrite files that have deletion vectors.
  2. Run VACUUM to delete the old files.

Time travel can still reach old versions until VACUUM removes the files.

Q54Criticalcompare

🔴 CRITICAL: When would you use Change Data Feed instead of time-travel diffs or full-table comparison? What does CDF store and expose, and what are its limits (retention, VACUUM, schema changes, cost)?

Expanded answer

Use CDF when I want row-level changes (insert, update, delete) from a Delta table, without comparing whole versions. It is good for incremental downstream updates.

What it stores. With delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true, Delta records change data for updates, deletes and merges in a _change_data folder. Insert-only commits can be computed from the log. It exposes the row plus metadata columns about the change type. See the CDF docs.

Limits.

  • Only changes after enabling are recorded.
  • Change data is kept only for the retention window. VACUUM removes it.
  • Reads use the latest table schema.
  • Tables with column mapping have restrictions.
  • There is a small storage cost.

Why not time-travel diffs. A diff of two versions reads two full snapshots. CDF reads only the changes.

Accuracy and gaps

Version note. Newer docs also describe an automatic change data feed that computes changes at read time using row lineage and needs no per-table setting. The classic one is now called "legacy". Both use the same read APIs. I checked the current docs before choosing.

Q55Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: Delta vs. plain Parquet: what exactly is Parquet missing? Give a concrete failure scenario that Delta handles and Parquet corrupts.

Expanded answer

Parquet is only a file format. It has no transaction log, no versions, no schema enforcement and no safe concurrent writes.

Failure scenario. A job writes 10 Parquet files and crashes after 6.

  • Plain Parquet folder: a reader sees 6 files. It reads half the data. No error.
  • Delta: the 6 files are not in the log, so no reader sees them. The table is unchanged. This is the atomic commit in the ACID docs.

Another case: two writers overwrite the same folder at once. Parquet gives mixed files. Delta fails one of them cleanly.

Q56Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: What happens to read performance if the transaction log grows to millions of commits? How do checkpoints and log compaction help?

Expanded answer

A reader has to replay every commit since the last checkpoint. With millions of commits and no checkpoint, that means listing and reading a huge number of JSON files. Table start-up gets slow.

  • Checkpoints save the full state at a version, so readers replay only the newer commits.
  • Log compaction merges a range of commit files into one, so there are fewer files to read.

Newer tables can use v2 checkpoints. Liquid clustering tables use them by default on newer runtimes, per the docs.

Q57Mediumcompare

🟡 MEDIUM: Compare INSERT OVERWRITE, replaceWhere, and dynamic partition overwrite vs. MERGE. What happens to old files, and how does each behave under a mid-write failure?

Expanded answer

Method What it replaces
INSERT OVERWRITE The whole table (or the partitions named)
replaceWhere Only rows that match my predicate
Dynamic partition overwrite Only the partitions that appear in the new data
MERGE Matched rows updated. Others inserted or left alone

Old files. All of them are marked removed in the log but stay on storage until VACUUM.

Mid-write failure. Every one of these is a single atomic commit. If the job fails before the commit, nothing changes for readers.

Q58Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A bad job corrupted a Silver table yesterday. How do you roll back with RESTORE, and what does it do to downstream streams, CDF consumers, and checkpoints?

Expanded answer

sql
DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.orders;                 -- find the good version
RESTORE TABLE silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF 42;

RESTORE creates a new commit that brings back the old version's files. The history goes forward. It does not erase the bad commit. The old data files must still exist, so I must not have run VACUUM past them.

Downstream effects (what I would check):

  • Streams reading this table see a commit that removes and re-adds files. A stream that expects append-only data can fail. I check options for handling non-append commits.
  • CDF consumers will see the restore as changes. They need to handle them.
  • Checkpoints of downstream streams still point to a version number, and the table keeps going forward, so they remain valid.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. The downstream effects above come from how the log works. I did not find a docs page that spells out every case, so I would test this in a non-production copy first.

Q59Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Where do Delta constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK) fit in a data quality strategy, and what are their limits?

Expanded answer

Fit. They are a last gate. A write that breaks a NOT NULL or CHECK rule fails the whole write. Good for rules that must never be broken.

Limits.

  • They fail the write. They do not send bad rows to quarantine.
  • They check one row at a time. No cross-row or cross-table rules.
  • Primary and foreign keys on Databricks are informational and not enforced.

For softer rules, with warnings or quarantine, I use pipeline expectations (Q84).

5Incremental / CDC / SCDQ60-69

Q60Criticalcode

🔴 CRITICAL: Implement SCD Type 2 with MERGE. Handle multiple changes to one key within a single batch, out-of-order events, and same-timestamp changes. What goes wrong with the naïve "update then insert" pattern?

Expanded answer

Idea. In SCD2, I keep every version of a row with effective_from, effective_to and is_current.

Plan.

  1. In staging, take all changes in the batch. Order per key by seq. Break ties with seq, not time.
  2. Build the full version chain for the batch. Each version's effective_to is the next version's effective_from.
  3. In one MERGE: close the current target row, and insert all the new versions.
sql
MERGE INTO dim_customer t
USING staged s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id AND t.effective_from = s.effective_from
WHEN MATCHED AND t.is_current AND s.effective_to IS NOT NULL
  THEN UPDATE SET t.effective_to = s.effective_to, t.is_current = false
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

What goes wrong with "update then insert" as two statements.

  • It is not atomic. A failure between them leaves a closed row and no new one.
  • A retry can create duplicates.
  • It cannot handle several changes for one key in a batch.
  • Out-of-order events produce wrong date ranges.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. The SQL is an outline of the pattern. I did not run it. The staging step (building the chain with LEAD) is where most of the real work sits.

Q61Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: A pipeline fails halfway and is retried. How do you ensure no duplicates and no data loss? Compare overwrite-by-partition, MERGE on a natural key, and transactional idempotent writes (e.g. txnAppId/txnVersion) as mechanisms.

Expanded answer

The goal: running the same batch twice gives the same result.

Mechanism How it is idempotent Good for Weak spot
Overwrite by partition (replaceWhere) A retry replaces the same slice Batch loads by date Needs clean partition boundaries
MERGE on natural key A retry updates the same rows Upserts Needs a unique key. Costly on big tables
txnAppId / txnVersion Delta remembers a write with the same app and version and skips it Appends and foreachBatch I must supply stable version numbers

Rule: the retry must reuse the same inputs, with the same batch ID or window.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. txnAppId and txnVersion are Delta idempotent-write options. I did not retrieve a docs page in this session, so I left them without a link. See the validation report.

Q62Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: How do you handle late-arriving and out-of-order CDC events, including deletes arriving before inserts? What role does a sequence column play, and how do you retain tombstones?

Expanded answer

Sequence column. It gives the true order of changes. I apply a change only if its sequence is higher than what the target has.

Delete before insert. I keep a tombstone: a delete marker with its sequence. When an older insert arrives later, its sequence is lower than the tombstone. So I ignore it.

Retaining tombstones. I keep them long enough to cover the biggest expected delay. In pipelines with AUTO CDC, the property pipelines.cdc.tombstoneGCThresholdInSeconds sets this. The Auto Loader docs say the default is two days. They also suggest soft deletes and comparing timestamps before updates.

Q63Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: You have five incremental strategies: watermark column, CDF, Auto Loader/streaming, snapshot diff, and log-based CDC. For a source with unreliable timestamps and hard deletes, which do you choose, what tradeoffs does it create, and what would change your decision?

Expanded answer

Strategy Unreliable timestamps? Hard deletes?
Watermark column Breaks Missed
CDF Fine, but source must be Delta Captured
Auto Loader / streaming Works for files Only if files carry deletes
Snapshot diff Fine Captured, but costly
Log-based CDC Fine Captured

My choice: log-based CDC. It reads the database's own change log. It does not use timestamps and it sees deletes.

Trade-offs. It needs setup on the source, access to the log, and a way to handle schema changes.

What would change my mind. If I cannot access the log, I use a snapshot diff on a schedule. If the source is already Delta, I use CDF.

Q64Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: What are the failure modes of a high-water-mark approach (long-running transactions, commit vs. updated_at, clock skew, missed deletes)? How do lookback windows and reconciliation checks help?

Expanded answer

Failure modes.

  • Long-running transaction. A row gets an updated_at before the transaction commits. I read past it, then it commits. I never see it.
  • Commit vs updated_at. The time the row is stamped is not the time it becomes visible.
  • Clock skew. Servers disagree on time.
  • Missed deletes. A deleted row leaves no timestamp.

Lookback window. I re-read the last N minutes or hours each run. Combined with an idempotent MERGE, duplicates are harmless and late commits are caught.

Reconciliation checks. I compare row counts and checksums between source and target on a schedule. If they differ, I investigate or re-sync that range.

Q65Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: Compare Lakeflow's AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES with a hand-written MERGE for SCD1/SCD2. What does the declarative option hide, and when would you still write MERGE?

Expanded answer

AUTO CDC. It is a streaming flow in Lakeflow pipelines. It supports SCD Type 1 and Type 2. The docs say it removes the need for code that handles out-of-order events, and for watermark concepts.

What it hides. Ordering logic, tombstone handling, and the exact MERGE steps. Less control. Harder to bend to special rules.

When I still write MERGE.

  • I need custom logic the declarative API does not support.
  • My target is not a pipeline table.
  • I must write into several tables from one batch.
  • I want full control of performance tuning.

Accuracy and gaps

Naming note. Older material calls this APPLY CHANGES. The current docs call it AUTO CDC. Both names appear in my question, so I keep both.

Q66Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: A source does hard deletes without CDC. How do you detect them? How do you propagate deletes (or a GDPR erasure) through Bronze, Silver, Gold, CDF, time travel, and VACUUM?

Expanded answer

Detect. Take a full list of keys from the source on a schedule. Anything in my table but missing in the source was deleted (an anti join).

Propagate.

  • Bronze: keep the raw history, or mark deleted keys.
  • Silver: apply a delete or set a soft-delete flag with MERGE.
  • Gold: rebuild or merge the same change.

GDPR erasure needs physical removal. The data also lives in:

  • CDF change files,
  • older versions (time travel),
  • deletion-vector files that still hold the old rows.

So I delete the rows, run REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) if deletion vectors are used, then VACUUM after the retention window. I do this in every layer.

Q67Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: Reprocess three months of data without corrupting Gold or breaking the live incremental run. How do you structure the replay?

Expanded answer

  1. Keep the live pipeline running and untouched.
  2. Replay into a separate shadow table with the same logic.
  3. Compare the shadow result to Gold on a sample.
  4. Swap in the replayed slices with replaceWhere for the date range. This is atomic.
  5. Use idempotent writes, so a re-run is safe.
  6. Avoid overlapping with the live job's partitions, or pause it for that range.
Q68Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you join facts to an SCD2 dimension for point-in-time accuracy, and what are the performance pitfalls?

Expanded answer

sql
SELECT f.*, d.segment
FROM fact f
JOIN dim d
  ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id
 AND f.event_ts >= d.effective_from
 AND f.event_ts <  d.effective_to;

This gives the dimension row that was valid at the event time.

Pitfalls. The range condition is a non-equi join. It is slower and can blow up if a key has many versions. Hot keys cause skew. Open-ended effective_to must be set to a far-future date, not NULL, or the range test fails.

Help. Filter the dimension early, keep the equality on key first, and consider pre-computing the surrogate key on the fact table.

Q69Highcode

🟠 HIGH: Given a Bronze CDC table (key, op, ts, seq, payload), write the MERGE that maintains a current-state Silver table including deletes and duplicates.

Follow-up: What if the same key has three updates in one micro-batch?

Follow-up: What if the batch is reprocessed?

Expanded answer

sql
MERGE INTO silver.customers t
USING (
  SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY seq DESC) rn
    FROM bronze.customers_cdc)
  WHERE rn = 1
) s
ON t.key = s.key
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' AND s.seq > t.seq THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' AND s.seq > t.seq THEN
  UPDATE SET t.payload = s.payload, t.seq = s.seq, t.ts = s.ts
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' THEN
  INSERT (key, payload, seq, ts) VALUES (s.key, s.payload, s.seq, s.ts);

Three updates for one key in one batch. The ROW_NUMBER step keeps only the latest by seq. The MERGE then sees one row per key, so there is no duplicate-match error (Q45).

Batch reprocessed. The s.seq > t.seq condition makes it safe. A replay changes nothing, since the target already has that sequence or higher.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. This is a pattern, not tested code. If hard deletes must stay visible to late events, I need a tombstone or soft-delete flag instead of DELETE (Q62).

6Streaming + Auto LoaderQ70-81

Q70Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: What exactly happens when a Structured Streaming job restarts? What is in the checkpoint (offsets, commits, state), and how does Spark decide what to reprocess?

Follow-up: What if the checkpoint is deleted or corrupted?

Follow-up: What if you change the query logic?

Expanded answer

What the checkpoint holds.

  • Offsets: what range of source data each micro-batch planned to read.
  • Commits: which batches finished.
  • State: saved data for stateful work such as aggregations and joins.

On restart. Spark reads the checkpoint. If the last planned batch has no commit, it re-runs that batch with the same offsets. Then it plans new batches after it.

Checkpoint deleted. The query starts as brand new. It forgets progress. I get reprocessing or gaps, based on where I tell it to start (for example startingVersion on a Delta source).

Checkpoint corrupted. I restore a backup, or start a new checkpoint at a version I know is safe. The CDF docs show an example of recovering from a corrupted checkpoint this way.

Query logic changed. Some changes are fine, such as a filter on stateless work. Changes that alter state (grouping keys, aggregations) are not allowed with the old checkpoint. Also, the shuffle partition setting cannot change between restarts of the same checkpoint.

Q71Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Does "exactly-once" mean duplicates are impossible? Explain what makes it true end to end, where it breaks (foreachBatch, external sinks, non-idempotent writes), and how you'd defend against it.

Expanded answer

No. "Exactly-once" is about processing, not about the data itself. Databricks says Structured Streaming guarantees exactly-once processing but does not deduplicate records from sources.

What makes it true end to end:

  1. A replayable source (offsets).
  2. A checkpoint that tracks progress.
  3. An idempotent or transactional sink, such as a Delta table.

Where it breaks:

  • foreachBatch: a batch can be retried, so non-idempotent writes duplicate data.
  • External sinks (APIs, databases) that cannot reject repeated writes.
  • The source itself sends duplicates.

Defence. Make writes idempotent (MERGE on a key, or txnAppId/txnVersion). Deduplicate within a watermark. Add unique IDs.

Q72Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Checkpoint vs. watermark: what problem does each solve? Give a scenario that confuses them.

Expanded answer

Checkpoint Watermark
Problem Recover progress and state after a restart Decide how late data can be, and clean old state
Lives in Storage location The query definition
If missing Query restarts from scratch State grows without limit

A confusing scenario. Late events arrive after a window closed. Someone deletes the checkpoint hoping to "reprocess" them. That does not help. The late data is a watermark problem. Deleting the checkpoint just resets progress and can create duplicates.

Q73Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: How do watermarks govern state cleanup and late data in a streaming aggregation? What happens to records that arrive after the watermark, and how do output modes change visible results? How would you deduplicate within a watermark?

Expanded answer

A watermark says "I wait this long for late data". Spark tracks the newest event time seen. State for a window is kept until the window's end is older than newest time minus the threshold. Then it is dropped.

python
(df.withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
   .groupBy(window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "id").count())

Late records. Records inside the threshold are processed correctly. Records after it may or may not be processed. There is no guarantee.

Output modes.

Mode Effect
Append A row is written only after the watermark passes. Results are delayed
Update Rows are written as soon as computed, and may be updated
