Complete All state is kept. The whole result is rewritten each trigger

Deduplicate. On Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above, dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark removes duplicates inside the threshold by a unique ID, even when other fields (like event time) differ.

Q74Mediumcompare

🟡 MEDIUM: Compare availableNow, processing-time, and continuous/low-latency triggers. When is availableNow on a schedule better than a always-on stream, or than a plain batch job?

Expanded answer

Trigger What it does Use when
availableNow Process everything available, then stop Scheduled incremental loads
Processing time (e.g. every 1 min) Run micro-batches on an interval, stays up Low latency, always on
Continuous / real-time mode Very low latency. Docs mention latency down to about five milliseconds Strict latency needs

availableNow vs always-on. It costs less because compute stops between runs.

availableNow vs plain batch. It remembers progress in the checkpoint, so I do not write my own "what is new" logic. This fits when 15-minute latency is fine (Q140).

Q75Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: How does Auto Loader discover files (directory listing vs. file notification/events)? What does it track in its checkpoint, how does it avoid reprocessing, and how does it scale to millions of files?

Expanded answer

Two ways to find new files (Auto Loader docs):

  • Directory listing. Auto Loader lists the folder to find new files. This is the default.
  • File notification. It uses storage events to learn about new files. Databricks recommends file notification with file events for most workloads.

What it tracks. It saves metadata of every discovered file in a key-value store (RocksDB) in the checkpoint. This is how each file is processed once. After a failure it resumes from there.

Scale. Discovery cost grows with the number of files ingested, not with how many folders they sit in. It supports near real-time ingestion of millions of files per hour.

Remember: Auto Loader does not guarantee file order.

Q76Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: A new column shows up in incoming JSON. Walk through Auto Loader schema inference, evolution modes, schemaLocation, and the rescued data column. What happens to the running stream, and how do you recover?

Expanded answer

Schema inference. Auto Loader samples data and infers a schema. It saves it in schemaLocation.

Evolution modes (cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode):

  • addNewColumns: add new columns to the schema.
  • rescue: keep the schema fixed. Put unknown fields in the rescued data column (_rescued_data).
  • failOnNewColumns: fail on a new column.
  • none: do not evolve. Unknown data goes to the rescued column if enabled.

What happens to the stream. In addNewColumns mode, the stream stops when it first sees a new column. The new schema is saved. When I restart, it picks up the new schema and continues.

Recovery. Run the job with retries so it restarts itself. The Lakeflow Jobs docs note that some features, such as schema evolution with Structured Streaming, assume jobs run with retries. Then check the downstream table. It must accept the new column (Q52).

Accuracy and gaps

Note. The mode names above come from my knowledge of Auto Loader. The retries claim is supported by the docs. I did not open the schema-evolution page itself in this session, so I would check the exact mode behaviour before relying on it.

Q77Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: Auto Loader vs. COPY INTO vs. plain batch reads vs. plain readStream on files. Under what conditions do you pick each, and what would flip the decision?

Expanded answer

Option Pick when
Auto Loader Files keep arriving, many files, need schema handling and scale
COPY INTO SQL-style, idempotent loads from a smaller set of files
Plain batch read One-off load or a fixed set of files
Plain readStream on files Small, simple case without schema evolution needs

Databricks lists the Auto Loader advantages over the plain file source: scalability, cost, and schema inference and evolution.

What flips it. Files grow to millions: move to Auto Loader. A one-time migration: use batch. The team prefers SQL and volumes are small: COPY INTO.

Q78Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: You use foreachBatch to MERGE into Silver. How do you ensure idempotency across micro-batch retries? What breaks if the batch function is non-deterministic or fails after partially committing?

Expanded answer

A micro-batch can run more than once. So the function must give the same result each time.

Make it idempotent:

  • Deduplicate the batch by key and sequence.
  • MERGE on a key. A repeat updates the same rows.
  • Compare sequence numbers so old data never overwrites new data.
  • For several writes, use txnAppId with the batch ID as txnVersion.

What breaks.

  • Non-deterministic function (random IDs, current_timestamp used as key): a retry creates different rows. Duplicates.
  • Partial commit: if the function writes to two tables and fails between, one table has the batch and the other does not. A retry then duplicates in the first. Use idempotent writes for each, or one transaction where supported.
Q79Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: Stream-static vs. stream-stream joins: how is state managed, why are watermarks required for stream-stream, and what staleness risks exist on the static side?

Expanded answer

Stream-static. The static side is a normal table. No join state is kept. Each micro-batch joins against the static table.

Stream-stream. Spark must remember rows from both sides until a match can arrive. That is join state.

Why watermarks. Without watermarks, Spark tries to join every key from both sides on each trigger, and state grows forever. Watermarks tell Spark when old state can be dropped. They are mandatory for outer joins, since they say when an unmatched key should be written with null.

Staleness on the static side. If the static table changes, the stream may use an old copy, depending on how it is read. A slowly changing lookup can give out-of-date results. I check when the static side refreshes.

Q80Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: How does the streaming state store (RocksDB) behave as state grows? How do you monitor and bound it?

Expanded answer

RocksDB keeps state on local disk and in memory buffers, so state can grow beyond heap memory. But bigger state means slower reads, longer commits and larger checkpoints.

Monitor. In the streaming query progress, I look at the state operator metrics: total rows in state, memory used and state commit times.

Bound it.

  • Use watermarks, so old state is dropped.
  • Avoid unbounded keys (like unique IDs without a time bound).
  • Use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark for deduplication.
Q81Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: A stream is falling behind. Which metrics in the streaming query progress tell you whether input rate or processing rate is the issue? How do maxFilesPerTrigger/maxBytesPerTrigger affect behavior?

Expanded answer

Compare two numbers in the progress report:

  • inputRowsPerSecond: how fast data arrives.
  • processedRowsPerSecond: how fast I process it.

If input is higher than processed, the stream is falling behind. I also read batch duration.

Rate limits. maxFilesPerTrigger and maxBytesPerTrigger cap how much one micro-batch reads.

  • Too high: large batches, spill, long latency.
  • Too low: many tiny batches and overhead.

I tune them so a batch finishes comfortably inside the trigger interval.

7Lakeflow + Medallion + ETLQ82-91

Q82Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Map the current Lakeflow ecosystem: Lakeflow Connect, Spark Declarative Pipelines, and Lakeflow Jobs. What role does each play, how does it relate to Delta Live Tables terminology you may see in older material, and where does Auto Loader fit?

Expanded answer

Piece Role
Lakeflow Connect Managed connectors to bring data in from sources
Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines Define transformations declaratively: streaming tables, materialized views, flows
Lakeflow Jobs Orchestrate tasks: dependencies, retries, schedules, repair runs
Auto Loader A streaming source (cloudFiles) for ingesting files. Used inside pipelines or plain streaming

Old names. Delta Live Tables (DLT) became Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and the current docs say Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. The docs say Lakeflow pipelines are built on Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines. Older code uses import dlt. Newer examples use dp. APPLY CHANGES became AUTO CDC.

Q83Criticalcompare

🔴 CRITICAL: Declarative vs. imperative pipelines: what do you gain and lose? Explain streaming tables vs. materialized views vs. views, and when a materialized view refresh is incremental vs. a full recompute.

Expanded answer

Gain from declarative: less code, automatic dependency order, automatic retries, built-in data quality and incremental processing. Lose: low-level control and some flexibility.

Dataset How it processes
Streaming table Each record processed once. Source should be append-only. Good for ingestion
Materialized view Recomputed as needed to match current data. Good for transformations and aggregations
View Not materialized. Only usable inside the same pipeline

These descriptions come from the pipeline docs.

Incremental or full recompute? The docs say a materialized view processes only new data and changes in the source tables whenever possible. When it cannot, it does a full recompute. It depends on the query and the sources. I check the pipeline event log to see which one happened.

Q84Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: How do expectations work (warn/drop/fail)? Where in the medallion would you place each, how would you build a quarantine pattern, and what can't expectations express?

Expanded answer

Expectations are SQL true/false rules on each record. Each needs a name and an action:

Action Result
warn (default) Bad rows are kept. Metrics are recorded
drop Bad rows are dropped before writing
fail The update fails. I must fix the issue before re-running

Placement (my view):

  • Bronze: warn. Keep everything, measure quality.
  • Silver: drop (with quarantine) for rows that should not move on.
  • Gold: fail for rules that must never be broken.

Quarantine pattern. Keep the clean rows with a drop expectation, and write the rows that break the rule to a separate table by using the inverse rule.

What expectations cannot express. The docs say constraints cannot contain custom Python functions, external calls, or subqueries on other tables.

Q85Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: What belongs in Bronze, Silver, and Gold? Name common mistakes (transforming in Bronze, Gold as a copy of Silver). When would you skip or add a layer, and how long would you retain Bronze to support replay?

Expanded answer

  • Bronze: raw data as it arrived, plus metadata. Append-only. This is my replay source.
  • Silver: cleaned, typed, deduplicated, conformed data.
  • Gold: business-ready tables for reporting and ML.

Common mistakes.

  • Transforming or filtering in Bronze. I lose the raw truth.
  • Gold that is just a copy of Silver. It adds cost with no value.
  • Business logic mixed into Silver.

Skip a layer for tiny, simple flows. Add a layer when many teams need an intermediate, shared model.

Bronze retention. Long enough to replay my longest correction window, and longer than the source keeps its own data. I size it from my replay needs.

Q86Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Design Bronze tables for a messy source: raw schema-as-strings vs. typed, ingestion metadata, rescued data, and append-only vs. upsert. Justify each choice.

Expanded answer

Choice My pick Why
Strings vs typed Raw payload kept, typed columns optional Bad values never cause a failed ingest
Ingestion metadata Source file, ingest time, batch ID Needed for replay and debugging
Rescued data Keep it Fields I did not expect are not lost
Append-only vs upsert Append-only Keeps full history. Dedupe belongs in Silver
Q87Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: ETL vs. ELT in a lakehouse: where does the "T" live now, and what does that change about governance and cost?

Expanded answer

ETL: transform before loading. ELT: load raw first, transform inside the platform.

In the lakehouse, the "T" lives in the lakehouse engine (Spark SQL or pipelines), after data lands in Bronze.

Governance. All layers sit in Unity Catalog, so one set of permissions and lineage applies. Cost. Compute runs for each transform step. Raw storage is cheap, but I pay compute to transform and to replay.

Q88Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A pipeline update fails midway. What state are the tables in? What is the risk of a full refresh on a streaming table when upstream source data has aged out, and how does selective refresh help?

Expanded answer

State of tables. Each table update is transactional. A table either has the new data or the old data. In a triggered pipeline, one failed flow does not fail other parallel flows. So some tables can be updated and some not.

Risk of full refresh. It clears the streaming table and reprocesses the source. If the source no longer has old data (a message queue with short retention, for example), that history is gone for good.

Selective refresh. I refresh only the flows or tables I choose. Databricks supports options like refresh_selection and full_refresh_selection in repairs, so I can avoid a full refresh on tables that cannot be rebuilt.

Q89Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: How does a pipeline infer dependencies between datasets? Compare triggered vs. continuous mode and development vs. production behavior.

Expanded answer

Dependencies. The pipeline analyzes my flows, tables and views to see what reads what. It orders and parallelizes execution on its own.

Triggered Continuous
Runs Once, then stops Keeps running
Cost Lower Higher, always on
Latency Higher Lower

Development vs production. Development mode is for quick iteration. Production mode is for reliability and retries. I check the current docs for the exact differences.

Q90Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: When would you use a managed Lakeflow Connect connector instead of custom ingestion code? What are the limits to check before committing?

Expanded answer

Use a managed connector when the source is supported and I do not want to build and run extraction, retries and CDC myself. The Databricks docs recommend Lakeflow Connect over federation when higher volumes and lower latency matter.

Check before committing:

  • Is my source and the objects I need supported?
  • API or rate limits on the source.
  • Latency and refresh schedule.
  • How it handles schema changes and deletes.
  • Cost.
Q91Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: How do you shape Gold for BI: star schema vs. wide denormalized tables vs. materialized views? How do refresh cost and freshness drive the choice?

Expanded answer

Shape Good for Cost
Star schema Reuse across many reports, clear model Joins at query time
Wide table Fast, simple dashboards More storage, harder to keep in sync
Materialized view Pre-computed aggregates Refresh cost, freshness limited by refresh

How I choose: more users and fast dashboards push me to pre-computed (wide or MV). A need for fresh data pushes me to smaller, more frequent refreshes. Many shared dimensions push me to a star schema.

8Unity Catalog + Governance + FederationQ92-101

Q92Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Describe the UC object model and privilege inheritance. Why does Unity Catalog give you governance that storage-level permissions alone cannot?

Expanded answer

Object model. Metastore → Catalog → Schema → Tables, views, volumes, functions and models. Names are catalog.schema.object.

Inheritance. A privilege granted on a catalog or schema applies to all current and future children. To read a table I also need USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA.

Why storage permissions are not enough. Storage permissions say who can read files. Unity Catalog says who can read tables, columns and rows. It adds audit, lineage, row filters, column masks, and one place for rules across many workspaces.

Q93Criticalcompare

🔴 CRITICAL: Managed vs. external tables and volumes: what happens on DROP, how do storage credentials and external locations fit, and why would you choose external despite managed being recommended?

Expanded answer

Managed External
Storage path Chosen by Unity Catalog Chosen by me
File lifecycle Managed by Unity Catalog Managed by me
On DROP Data files are deleted Only metadata is removed. Files stay

Per the docs, dropping a managed table deletes the data files. External tables keep them.

Credentials and locations. An external location ties a cloud path to a storage credential. Unity Catalog uses them to check who can reach the path. External tables and volumes must be in a path covered by an external location.

Why external despite the recommendation. Other systems write or read the same files. Data already exists in a fixed location. I need direct control over storage layout or lifecycle.

Accuracy and gaps

Doc wording differs. One docs page says managed table files are deleted after an 8-day retention period. Another says tables can be recovered with UNDROP for about 7 days. I would check the current docs before I depend on the exact number.

Q94Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A user has SELECT on a table but the query fails. List the possible causes (USE CATALOG/SCHEMA, external location, compute access mode, row filters/masks, workspace binding) and your diagnostic order.

Expanded answer

My order, from cheapest to check:

  1. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA missing on the parents.
  2. Workspace binding. The catalog may not be bound to this workspace.
  3. Compute access mode. The cluster's mode may not support this feature or table type.
  4. External location or credential. For external data, the path access must work.
  5. Row filters and column masks. They may hide data, or fail through the function.
  6. Views. The view owner may lack access to what the view reads.
  7. Network or firewall to the storage.
Q95Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Design Unity Catalog governance for multiple teams and environments: catalog layout, ownership, groups, service principals, and workspace bindings. What tradeoffs does your layout create?

Expanded answer

Layout (my proposal):

  • One catalog per environment and domain, for example prod_sales, dev_sales.
  • Schemas for layers (bronze, silver, gold) or subdomains.
  • Owners are groups, not people.
  • Production jobs run as service principals.
  • Workspace bindings restrict prod catalogs to prod workspaces.

Trade-offs.

Choice Benefit Cost
More catalogs Strong isolation More objects to manage
Fewer catalogs Simple Broad inherited grants
Strict bindings Safer Less flexible for cross-team work
Q96Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: Compare row filters, column masks, and dynamic views for fine-grained access. What are the performance and maintenance tradeoffs?

Expanded answer

What it does Trade-off
Row filter Hides rows based on the user Applied on the table. One place to maintain. Function runs on queries
Column mask Replaces a column's values for some users Same, per column
Dynamic view A view with user-based logic Easy to start, but rules are spread across many views

Rules on the table (filters and masks) are harder to bypass, since users cannot read the raw table. Functions run per query, so keep them simple. I did not find a docs page in this session for exact performance numbers, so I do not quote any.

Q97Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: What do lineage and audit system tables capture? What are their blind spots? How would you use them for impact analysis before changing a column?

Expanded answer

Lineage shows which tables and columns feed which others. Audit shows who did what, and when.

Blind spots. They only capture activity that goes through Unity Catalog. Work done outside it, such as by path or by external tools, may be missing.

Impact analysis. Before I change a column, I query column lineage for everything that reads it. Then I check the owners and jobs of those assets and warn them.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. I did not retrieve the system-table docs in this session, so I list the exact table names under "Documentation links to verify".

Q98Criticalcompare

🔴 CRITICAL: When is federation preferable to ingestion, and when is it a bad choice? Cover pushdown, performance, source load, freshness, governance, and cost. Include the difference between query federation and catalog federation.

Expanded answer

Two kinds (Lakehouse Federation docs):

Query federation Catalog federation
Path Query is pushed down to the external database over JDBC Query runs directly on the files in object storage
Compute Databricks and the remote database Databricks only
Writes Read-only Read-only
Cost and speed Depends on the remote system More cost-effective than query federation

Federation is preferable for ad hoc reports, proofs of concept, live access with minimal data movement, and moving to Unity Catalog step by step.

It is a bad choice for heavy repeated queries (they load the source system), low-latency or high-volume needs (the docs recommend Lakeflow Connect there), and big cross-source joins.

Compare:

  • Freshness: federation is live. Ingestion is as fresh as the last load.
  • Source load: federation adds it. Ingestion loads once.
  • Governance: both use Unity Catalog foreign catalogs.
Q99Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you migrate from Hive metastore, mounts, and DBFS paths to UC, volumes, and external locations? What breaks along the way?

Expanded answer

Plan.

  1. Move tables from Hive metastore to Unity Catalog (managed or external).
  2. Replace mounts with external locations and volumes.
  3. Replace dbfs:/ paths in code with volume paths or table names.

The docs call DBFS root and mounts a deprecated pattern.

What breaks. Hard-coded paths. Two-level table names that need a catalog. Jobs that relied on cluster-level credentials. Libraries or features that do not work on some compute modes.

Q100Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: When is Delta Sharing the right alternative to copying data?

Expanded answer

When I need to give someone live, read-only access to my data without making a copy. It fits sharing with other teams, companies or platforms. The data stays in one place and stays current. Recipients cannot write to it. I should still copy the data if the recipient needs to change it or needs very different retention.

Q101Mediumconcept

🟡 MEDIUM: How are federation connection credentials stored and scoped? Who can use a connection, and how do you avoid a shared super-user credential?

Expanded answer

A connection is a Unity Catalog object that holds the path and credentials of the external system. Users do not see the credential. Access is controlled by Unity Catalog privileges on the connection and on the foreign catalog.

Avoid a shared super-user.

  • Create separate connections per team or purpose.
  • Use a least-privilege account on the source for each.
  • Grant the connection to groups, not individuals.
  • Rotate credentials, and prefer OAuth when the source supports it.

9Compute + PhotonQ102-107

Q102Criticalconcept

🔴 CRITICAL: Does Photon replace Spark? What does it actually accelerate, what falls back, and why can a query remain slow with Photon (I/O bound, skew, shuffle, Python UDFs, driver-bound work)?

Expanded answer

No. Catalyst still plans the query. Photon takes over the execution of supported operators, using a native C++ engine that works on batches of rows.

What it speeds up. Scans, filters, hash aggregates, hash joins, shuffles, and writes (including UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE). It works best on longer queries over large data.

What falls back to Spark. Unsupported operations. The docs list UDFs, RDD APIs and Dataset APIs as unsupported. Stateful streaming is not supported either. Queries that normally run in under two seconds see little gain.

Why a query can stay slow with Photon:

  • It is I/O bound (slow storage or many small files).
  • It has skew. One task still has too much data.
  • Shuffle volume is huge.
  • A Python UDF forces a fallback.
  • The time goes on the driver (planning, collect).
Q103Highcompare

🟠 HIGH: For a production ETL job, compare classic job compute, serverless jobs compute, and a SQL warehouse. Consider cost, startup time, isolation, tuning control, and what you lose with serverless.

Expanded answer

Classic job compute Serverless jobs SQL warehouse
Start-up Minutes to start a cluster Fast Fast (serverless) or slower
Tuning control Highest (instance types, Spark configs, init scripts) Low Size and scaling only
Isolation My own VMs Databricks-managed isolation Shared warehouse
Cost shape DBUs plus my cloud VMs Usage-based Per warehouse size and time
Best for Heavy or custom ETL Simple low-ops ETL SQL-only transformations

What I lose with serverless. Custom VM choices, some Spark settings and some libraries or low-level control. It is the trade-off in Q1. See the serverless docs for current limits.

Q104Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: How would you size compute for a 2 TB daily job? Cover memory- vs. compute-optimized instances, autoscaling pitfalls with shuffle-heavy work, spot instances, and pools.

Expanded answer

Start from the work, not the size. Is it scan-heavy, shuffle-heavy or memory-heavy? I test on a sample, then scale up.

  • Memory-optimized instances: joins, wide aggregations, caching, spill.
  • Compute-optimized instances: CPU-heavy transforms.
  • Autoscaling pitfalls. Removing workers in a shuffle-heavy job loses their shuffle files, so work is recomputed. For stable shuffle jobs I prefer a fixed size, or a gentle scale-down.
  • Spot instances. Cheaper, but they can be taken away. Use on-demand for the driver. Expect more retries.
  • Pools. Pre-warmed instances cut start-up time.

I check the Spark UI for spill and idle cores to see if I sized right.

Q105Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A SQL warehouse is slow under concurrency. How do sizing, cluster scaling, queueing, caching, and the query profile inform your diagnosis?

Expanded answer

  1. Queueing. Are queries waiting? If yes, I need more clusters (scaling) rather than a bigger size.
  2. Sizing. If single queries are slow even with no queue, the warehouse is too small for the query, or the query is bad.
  3. Caching. Repeated dashboard queries should hit a cache. If not, I check why.
  4. Query profile. I look at where time goes: scan, shuffle, spill, or waiting.

Rule of thumb: queueing means add clusters. Slow single queries mean look at the query or the size.

Q106Mediumcompare

🟡 MEDIUM: Compare standard and dedicated access modes. What do they imply for UC enforcement, libraries, and language support?

Expanded answer

  • Standard (shared): many users on one cluster, with isolation between them. Unity Catalog is enforced per user. Some features are restricted for safety.
  • Dedicated: one user or group owns it. It supports more libraries and low-level features.

I pick standard when many users share compute and I want enforced isolation. I pick dedicated when I need features that standard blocks.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. I wrote this from general knowledge. I did not retrieve the access-mode docs, so the exact language and library limits are not listed. See the validation report.

Q107Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you attribute and control cost (system billing tables, tags, budget policies, cluster policies)? What are the top three cost mistakes in Databricks?

Expanded answer

Attribute. Tag compute and jobs. Query the system billing tables by tag, job and workspace.

Control. Cluster policies limit sizes and types. Budget policies track spend per team.

Top three mistakes (my view):

  1. Always-on clusters or warehouses left running.
  2. Over-sized compute for small jobs, with no auto-termination.
  3. Running everything on all-purpose compute instead of job compute.

10Performance + TroubleshootingQ108-122

Q108Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: A large Delta MERGE takes hours. Diagnose it, explain what's happening internally, identify shuffle/skew/file-layout issues, and describe how you'd validate the fix.

Expanded answer

Internals. MERGE joins source and target to find touched files, then rewrites them (Q44).

Diagnose in order:

  1. Table history: compare scan time and rewrite time, and the number of files rewritten.
  2. Spark UI: shuffle size, skew in the join stage, spill.
  3. Source: duplicates? Size? Is it deduplicated?
  4. Target layout: is it clustered or partitioned by the merge key? Many small files or huge files?

Fixes. Add a partition or cluster predicate to the ON clause. Enable deletion vectors. Fix skew. Compact files. Dedupe the source.

Validate. Same input, before and after. Same row counts and checksum. Compare run time and files rewritten (Q110).

Q109Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: A job with unchanged code runs 10x slower this week. What changed? Lay out your investigation plan across data volume, skew, file layout, cluster, runtime, concurrency, and plan changes.

Expanded answer

Check What I look at
Data volume Input size, row counts this week vs last
Skew Task duration spread in the slowest stage
File layout Many small files? Missed OPTIMIZE?
Cluster Node types, autoscaling, spot loss
Runtime Runtime version change
Concurrency Other jobs on the same compute or table
Plan Compare EXPLAIN now vs an old run

I compare the slowest stage this week to the same stage last week. The difference points to the cause.

Q110Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: How would you prove a performance optimization actually worked? Address cold vs. warm cache, noisy neighbors, data variance, the metrics you'd compare, and how you'd confirm the plan really changed.

Expanded answer

  • Same data, same input snapshot, before and after.
  • Cold vs warm cache. Compare cold with cold and warm with warm. Disk cache can make the second run look faster for no real reason.
  • Noisy neighbours. Run several times, on isolated compute, and use the median.
  • Metrics. Total time, shuffle bytes, spill, files read, bytes read, tasks.
  • Confirm the plan changed. Compare EXPLAIN before and after. A new join type or fewer files scanned proves the change took effect.
  • Check results are identical.
Q111Criticaltroubleshooting

🔴 CRITICAL: Compare an executor OOM and a driver OOM. What typically causes each in real pipelines, and what exact steps do you take to diagnose and fix them?

Expanded answer

Executor OOM Driver OOM
Typical cause Skew, huge partitions, big joins, UDF memory collect(), toPandas(), large broadcast, huge file listing
Evidence Failed tasks, "executor lost", high GC Driver error, driver memory chart high
First step Find the failing stage and the biggest task Find the line that pulls data to the driver
Fix More partitions, fix skew, more memory per task Remove collect, write to storage, shrink the broadcast
Q112Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: What do you look at in the Spark UI (stage summary, task metrics, shuffle read/write, spill, GC time, input size) to classify a problem as skew, spill, small files, or bad plan?

Expanded answer

Problem Spark UI signal
Skew Max task much larger than median (shuffle read or duration)
Spill Spill memory and disk columns are non-zero
Small files Thousands of tiny tasks, small input per task, long scheduling time
Bad plan Wrong join type, full scan, extra shuffles in the SQL tab
GC GC time is a big share of task time
Q113Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: Pushdown and pruning are not happening even though your filter looks selective. What could prevent them (casts, functions on columns, UDFs, partition-column misuse), and how do you verify the fix?

Expanded answer

What blocks them:

  • A cast or function on the column (WHERE cast(id as string) = '5').
  • A UDF in the filter.
  • Filtering on a derived column instead of the partition column.
  • A type mismatch between the column and the literal.

Fix. Rewrite so the bare column is compared to a literal of the right type.

Verify. Read the plan (Q16). The filter should appear in the scan's pushed filters or partition filters, and the bytes read should drop.

Q114Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A job produces millions of tiny tasks and files. Diagnose it on both the read side and write side, and fix it without creating a new bottleneck.

Expanded answer

Read side. Many tiny source files make one task per file. Fix: compact the source with OPTIMIZE, or use bigger input splits.

Write side. Too many partitions or too many write tasks create tiny output files. Fix: coalesce or repartition before the write, or use optimized writes and auto compaction (Q51).

Avoid a new bottleneck. Do not coalesce to one partition. Aim for sensible file sizes, and keep enough parallelism.

Q115Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Describe how partitioning can hurt performance (over-partitioning, skew, mismatch with repartition before partitionBy, high-cardinality columns). How do you decide whether to partition at all?

Expanded answer

How it hurts.

  • Over-partitioning / high cardinality: thousands of folders with tiny files.
  • Skew: one partition holds most of the data.
  • Mismatch: writing with partitionBy without a matching repartition makes each task write to many partitions, so tiny files appear.

Decide whether to partition. I partition only if the table is very large, the column is low-cardinality, and queries filter on it. Otherwise I use liquid clustering. See Q49.

Q116Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: Duplicates appear in a Silver table fed by a stream. Diagnose the possible causes (source, restart, foreachBatch, non-idempotent MERGE, replays) and show how to prove which one it is.

Expanded answer

Suspect How I prove it
Source duplicates The same business key appears in Bronze more than once
Restart / replay Duplicates share the same source offset or file, from different batch IDs
foreachBatch retry Duplicates share a batch ID, with a failed then retried run
Non-idempotent MERGE Source has duplicate keys, or no sequence check
Manual reprocess Table history shows an extra write at that time

I use DESCRIBE HISTORY, a GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, and the metadata columns (file, ingest time, batch ID) that I stored in Bronze.

Q117Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: An Auto Loader stream stops picking up new files, or fails on schema change. Walk through diagnosis and recovery.

Expanded answer

Not picking up files.

  1. Check the stream is running, and the query progress.
  2. Check the source path, and file permissions.
  3. In file notification mode, check the event setup.
  4. Check whether files were already seen (they are tracked in the checkpoint).
  5. Check for naming or path filters.

Schema change failure. The stream stops in addNewColumns mode. Restart it, and it picks up the new schema (Q76). Run the job with retries.

Recovery. If the checkpoint is damaged, start a new one and decide carefully what to backfill.

Q118Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: A Lakeflow pipeline fails after a source schema change. What do you inspect, how do you recover, and how do you prevent a repeat?

Expanded answer

Inspect. The pipeline event log and the failing flow's error. Compare the old and new source schema.

Recover. Fix the code or schema handling for the new column. Re-run the update. Use a selective refresh, not a full refresh, when old source data may be gone (Q88).

Prevent. Keep a rescued-data column. Agree on data contracts with the source team (Q139). Add expectations that check the schema.

Q119Hightroubleshooting

🟠 HIGH: You see FetchFailed / "executor lost" / missing shuffle blocks. List the causes (spot loss, OOM kill, disk, network) and the remedies for each.

Expanded answer

Cause Remedy
Spot instance taken away Use on-demand for stable work, or accept retries
OOM kill of the executor More memory per task, fix skew
Disk full on the executor Bigger disks, reduce spill and shuffle
Network problems Retry, check the network, reduce shuffle size
Autoscaling removed a worker Slow down scale-down, or use a fixed size

All of them lose shuffle files. Spark reruns the map tasks (Q21).

Q120Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: A join produces correct counts in dev and exploding counts in prod. How do you find the cause?

Expanded answer

In prod the join key has duplicates that dev did not have. I check key uniqueness on both sides with GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. I also check for null keys and for different data. See Q32.

Q121Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: A dashboard query on a SQL warehouse is slow. What do you read in the query profile, and what are your first three fixes?

Expanded answer

In the query profile I read where time goes (scan, shuffle, join), the bytes and files read, spill, and the Photon share.

First three fixes:

  1. Reduce data read: cluster by the filter columns, filter early.
  2. Fix the join or add pre-aggregation (materialized view or Gold table).
  3. Resize the warehouse or scale clusters if it is queueing.
Q122Mediumtroubleshooting

🟡 MEDIUM: Users see stale results after a table update. Compare Spark cache, disk cache, and query result cache, and explain how each can mislead.

Expanded answer

Cache What it holds How it can mislead
Spark cache A computed DataFrame in a session Keeps an old result until I refresh or unpersist
Disk cache Copies of data files on local SSD Can show older files for a short time
Query result cache The final result of a query Can return an old result until it is invalidated

I check which cache is in play, then refresh or clear it.

11Jobs / Workflows / DeploymentQ123-127

Q123Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Design a Lakeflow Job with task dependencies, retries, parameters, and repair runs. What happens if a retried task is not idempotent, and how do you design for it?

Expanded answer

Design.

  • Tasks with dependencies: ingest → transform → publish.
  • Retries on transient failures.
  • Job parameters, such as run date, to keep tasks reusable.
  • Alerts on failure.

Repair runs. A repair re-runs only failed tasks and their dependents. Successful tasks are not re-run.

If a retried task is not idempotent. The docs warn that Lakeflow Jobs does not make tasks idempotent. A task that wrote partial output can duplicate data on re-run.

Design for it. Use overwrite-by-partition, or MERGE, instead of append. Key each run by the run date.

Q124Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Describe a dev/test/prod promotion flow with Git, Databricks Asset Bundles, and CI/CD. How do you handle environment-specific config, catalogs, and testing?

Expanded answer

  1. Code lives in Git. A pull request triggers CI.
  2. CI runs unit tests, then bundle validate.
  3. Databricks Asset Bundles define jobs and pipelines as code, with targets for dev, test and prod.
  4. CI deploys to test. After checks, it deploys to prod using a service principal.

Environment config. Each target sets its own workspace, catalog and variables. The code stays the same.

Testing. Unit tests for logic. Integration tests run in test using test data.

Accuracy and gaps

Naming note. One third-party blog says the feature was renamed "Declarative Automation Bundles" in 2026. I could not confirm that in the official docs I opened. They still say "Asset Bundles", so I use that name.

Q125Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Where do secrets live (secret scopes, UC connections, service principal OAuth)? How do you handle rotation, and which identity should production jobs run as?

Expanded answer

  • Secret scopes store keys and passwords for my code.
  • UC connections store credentials for federation (Q101).
  • Service principal OAuth lets jobs authenticate without personal tokens.

Rotation. Update the secret in one place. Code reads it at run time, so no code change.

Identity. Production jobs run as a service principal, not a person. A person leaving does not break the job.

Q126Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you make pipelines reproducible (pinned runtimes, library versions, wheels) and testable (unit tests for PySpark transformations)?

Expanded answer

Reproducible. Pin the runtime version. Pin library versions. Build my code as a wheel and deploy that exact file.

Testable. Write transformations as functions that take and return DataFrames. Test them with small input DataFrames and expected output.

Q127Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How would you monitor and alert on job duration, failures, and data freshness? Which signals would you track beyond "job succeeded"?

Expanded answer

Track:

  • Job duration against its normal range.
  • Failures and retries.
  • Freshness: the newest timestamp in the table versus now.
  • Volume: row counts against expected.
  • Quality: expectation metrics, quarantine counts.
  • Cost.

A job can succeed and still deliver empty or stale data. So freshness and volume checks matter most.

12APIs + SalesforceQ128-133

Q128Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Design incremental Lead extraction from Salesforce. Cover SystemModstamp vs. LastModifiedDate, REST vs. Bulk API, pagination, handling deletes, and daily API limits.

Expanded answer

Cursor field. I use SystemModstamp. It also changes when system processes update a record. LastModifiedDate changes only on user edits, so I can miss changes.

REST vs Bulk. REST for small or moderate sets. Bulk API for large volumes. It uses fewer API calls.

Pagination. Follow the next-records link, or use Bulk result sets. Save progress per page or batch.

Deletes. Query deleted records (an IsDeleted filter, or the deleted-records endpoint) and mark them in my table.

Limits. Count API calls against the daily quota. Prefer Bulk. Use a lookback window and an idempotent MERGE.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. Salesforce is not Databricks, and I did not retrieve Salesforce docs in this session. I list them under "Documentation links to verify". I wrote the field behaviour from general knowledge.

Q129Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Salesforce returns rate-limit errors, a 401 mid-extract, and a partial batch failure. Describe retry/backoff, token refresh, checkpointing of progress, and how you keep the extraction idempotent.

Expanded answer

Event What I do
Rate limit (429 or limit error) Wait with exponential backoff and retry
401 (token expired) Refresh the token once, then retry. Do not loop forever
Partial batch failure Re-process only the failed records

Checkpointing. After each successful page or batch, save the cursor value and batch ID.

Idempotency. Land data with the extract time and cursor. Load with MERGE by record ID. A repeat gives the same result.

Q130Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: You write scored Leads back to Salesforce. Cover upsert by external ID, Bulk API partial failures, duplicate prevention, record locking, triggers/flows reacting to your writes, and audit/replay.

Expanded answer

  • Upsert by external ID. I use an external ID field so a repeat updates the same Lead, not a new one.
  • Partial failures. Bulk results list each failed record. I store them with the error and retry only those.
  • Duplicate prevention. The external ID, and deduplication before sending.
  • Record locking. Many parallel writes to the same parent can lock. Use smaller batches and order by parent.
  • Triggers and flows. My writes can fire them. I agree with the Salesforce admins first, and write only the fields I own.
  • Audit and replay. Keep a table of every payload sent with run ID and result.
Q131Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: simple-salesforce runs on the driver. What does that mean for parallelism, memory, and failure handling at scale? When do you move to Bulk API, a managed connector, or a distributed approach?

Expanded answer

Code that uses simple-salesforce runs on the driver only. So:

  • Parallelism: none from Spark. One machine does the calls.
  • Memory: all rows go through the driver, so big pulls can run out of memory.
  • Failures: if the driver dies, the job restarts.

When I move. For large volumes, I use the Bulk API. If a managed connector supports Salesforce, I use Lakeflow Connect where it fits. For custom needs, I split the work into ID ranges and process them in parallel on executors.

Q132Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Salesforce admins add custom fields, change types, or delete fields. How does your Bronze/Silver design absorb that without breaking the pipeline?

Expanded answer

Bronze. Store the raw record (JSON or a map) plus extraction metadata. New fields land safely in the raw payload.

Silver. Select a fixed list of columns I know. New fields do not break it. A check alerts me when new fields appear. For type changes, I cast safely and send bad values to quarantine. For deleted fields, I allow nulls.

Q133Mediumcompare

🟡 MEDIUM: Compare the OAuth flows usable for server-to-server Salesforce access (JWT bearer, client credentials, username-password+token). What are the security tradeoffs, and how do you handle tokens safely in distributed code?

Expanded answer

Flow Security
JWT bearer Strong. Uses a certificate and no password. Good for servers
Client credentials Good. App secret only, tied to a run-as user
Username + password + token Weakest. Passwords and a person's identity are involved

Handling tokens. Keep secrets in secret scopes. Never print or log tokens. Request a token on the driver, or per task if needed, and refresh when it expires. Do not put tokens in notebooks or code.

13Architecture / System DesignQ134-141

Q134Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Design the full Salesforce → Databricks → Salesforce loop with rule-based lead scoring. Cover ingestion, storage layers, transformation, compute, governance, orchestration, monitoring, failure recovery, and performance.

Expanded answer

  • Ingestion. Incremental extract with a cursor, Bulk API (Q128).
  • Storage. Bronze raw leads, Silver cleaned leads, Gold scored leads.
  • Transformation. Scoring rules as SQL or PySpark functions, with tests.
  • Compute. Job compute or serverless jobs.
  • Governance. Unity Catalog, with PII columns masked.
  • Orchestration. A Lakeflow Job: extract → bronze → silver → score → write back.
  • Write-back. Upsert by external ID with failure logs (Q130).
  • Monitoring. Freshness, volume, failed write-back counts.
  • Recovery. Idempotent steps, repair runs, replay from Bronze.
  • Performance. Incremental loads only, small output sets for write-back.
Q135Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Design a fault-tolerant incremental batch ingestion platform for ~200 heterogeneous sources. How do you handle onboarding, schema drift, rerunnability, quarantine, replay, and cost?

Expanded answer

  • Onboarding. A config table drives each source: type, cursor, schedule, target. A new source means a new row, not new code.
  • Schema drift. Raw payload plus rescued data in Bronze.
  • Rerunnability. Idempotent loads (MERGE or replace-by-partition).
  • Quarantine. Bad records go to a quarantine table with reason and source.
  • Replay. Bronze is the replay source.
  • Cost. Group sources into a few jobs, use job compute or serverless, and use incremental loads.
Q136Criticaldesign

🔴 CRITICAL: Design a streaming lakehouse with late data, schema evolution, and the ability to replay. Where do you use watermarks, checkpoints, and idempotent writes, and what is your recovery plan?

Expanded answer

  • Ingestion: Auto Loader or a message source into Bronze.
  • Watermarks: in Silver and Gold aggregations, to handle late data and bound state (Q73).
  • Checkpoints: one per stream, stored safely and backed up (Q70).
  • Schema evolution: rescued data column, controlled evolution (Q76).
  • Idempotent writes: MERGE or txnAppId/txnVersion in foreachBatch (Q78).
  • Replay: Bronze is append-only, so I can re-run from it.
  • Recovery: restart from the checkpoint. If lost, start a new checkpoint from a known version.
Q137Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Design a pipeline that processes billions of records daily with an SLA. Cover layout (partitioning vs. clustering), compute, incremental strategy, skew, cost, and how you'd prove it meets the SLA.

Expanded answer

  • Layout. Liquid clustering on common filter and join keys.
  • Compute. Sized for peak with room to spare. Photon on.
  • Incremental. Process only new data. Do not recompute history.
  • Skew. Use AQE, and handle hot keys with the tools in Q26.
  • Cost. Job compute, right-sized, auto-terminate.
  • Prove the SLA. Track run duration over many days. Check the 95th percentile, not the average. Alert when it comes close.
Q138Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Design CDC from an OLTP database into SCD2 Silver tables, including deletes, schema evolution, ordering guarantees, and backfill.

Expanded answer

  1. Capture changes from the database log into Bronze (with key, op, ts, seq).
  2. Apply ordering by sequence per key.
  3. Build SCD2 versions (Q60), or use AUTO CDC with SCD type 2 (Q65).
  4. Deletes: close the current version, or keep a tombstone.
  5. Schema evolution: rescued data and controlled column adds.
  6. Backfill: take a snapshot, load it, then start the change stream from its position.
Q139Highdesign

🟠 HIGH: Design schema evolution and data contracts across Bronze, Silver, and Gold so that an upstream change doesn't silently break consumers.

Expanded answer

  • Bronze: accept everything. Keep raw and rescued data.
  • Silver: a fixed schema, enforced. New columns need a review.
  • Gold: a stable, versioned interface for consumers.
  • Data contract: a written agreement with the producer on columns, types, and change notice.
  • Checks: expectations for schema and nullability. Alerts on a change.
Q140Mediumcompare

🟡 MEDIUM: A business wants "near real time" but 15-minute latency is acceptable. Choose among streaming, availableNow micro-batches, and frequent batch, with cost and operational tradeoffs.

Expanded answer

Option Cost Operations
Always-on streaming Highest Needs monitoring around the clock
availableNow every 15 min Low (compute stops between runs) Simple, with progress tracked by the checkpoint
Frequent plain batch Low I write my own "what is new" logic

My pick: availableNow on a 15-minute schedule. It is cheap and keeps progress state for me (Q74).

Q141Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How would you design disaster recovery and multi-region resilience for the lakehouse (data, metadata, jobs, identity)?

Expanded answer

  • Data: replicate storage to a second region.
  • Metadata: back up or replicate the catalog definitions.
  • Jobs: keep jobs as code (bundles) so I can redeploy in the other region.
  • Identity: manage users and groups centrally and replicate them.
  • Test it. A plan I never rehearsed is not a plan.

Accuracy and gaps

Note. I did not retrieve Databricks DR documentation in this session. This is a general design outline. See the validation report.

14ML / AI / MLflow / RAGQ142-145

Q142Highconcept

🟠 HIGH: Explain MLflow tracking vs. model registry (with UC), and how experiment tracking supports reproducibility and promotion to serving.

Expanded answer

  • Tracking: records each run: parameters, metrics, code version, artifacts.
  • Model registry (with Unity Catalog): stores model versions, with governance, aliases and lineage.

Reproducibility. A run holds what I need to repeat training. Promotion. I register the best run's model, test it, assign an alias such as "champion", and serve from that alias.

Q143Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: How do you avoid training-serving skew when engineering features at scale on Databricks?

Expanded answer

Skew happens when features are computed one way for training and another way for serving.

Avoid it. Define each feature once, in one shared code path or feature table. Use it for both training and serving. Test that training and serving features match.

Q144Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: Outline a RAG pipeline on Databricks (ingest, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, serve). How do you handle freshness, governance, and evaluation?

Expanded answer

Pipeline: ingest documents → split into chunks → embed → store in a vector index → retrieve top matches → pass them to the model → serve the answer.

  • Freshness: re-ingest changed documents on a schedule.
  • Governance: Unity Catalog permissions on source data, and keep access rules in the retrieval step.
  • Evaluation: a fixed set of questions with known good answers. Check retrieval quality and answer quality.
Q145Mediumdesign

🟡 MEDIUM: When would you replace a rule-based lead-scoring system with an ML model? How would you evaluate it and productionize it?

Expanded answer

Replace when rules no longer capture the patterns, there is enough labelled history (leads that did or did not convert), and the rules cost too much to maintain.

Evaluate. Compare the model with the rules on held-out data. Check precision, recall and lift on top leads. Run both side by side before switching.

Productionize. Track runs with MLflow, register the model in Unity Catalog, run batch scoring in a job, write scores back (Q130), and monitor drift.

15LAST 30-MINUTE RAPID-FIRE QUESTIONSRapid-fire

Rapid 1Untaggedrapid

What causes a shuffle?

Expanded answer

Operations that need the same keys together: groupBy, joins, distinct, window, orderBy, repartition (Q10).

Rapid 2Untaggedrapid

When would you broadcast?

Expanded answer

When one side of a join is small enough to copy to every executor (Q13).

Rapid 3Untaggedrapid

Repartition vs. coalesce?

Expanded answer

repartition shuffles and can grow or balance. coalesce merges without a shuffle and only reduces (Q11).

Rapid 4Untaggedrapid

What does AQE change at runtime?

Expanded answer

Join type, number of shuffle partitions, skewed partitions, and empty relations, using real shuffle sizes (Q15).

Rapid 5Untaggedrapid

What does Photon replace, and what does it not?

Expanded answer

It replaces the execution of supported operators. It does not replace Catalyst planning or Spark itself, and it does not run UDFs (Q102).

Rapid 6Untaggedrapid

What is stored in the Delta transaction log?

Expanded answer

Commits with actions (add, remove, metaData, protocol, commitInfo) and periodic checkpoints (Q42).

Rapid 7Untaggedrapid

What happens when a MERGE source has duplicate keys?

Expanded answer

An update fails with a multiple-match error. An unconditional delete is allowed (Q45).

Rapid 8Untaggedrapid

CDF vs. time travel?

Expanded answer

CDF gives row-level changes. Time travel gives whole old versions (Q54).

Rapid 9Untaggedrapid

Checkpoint vs. watermark?

Expanded answer

Checkpoint saves progress and state. Watermark sets lateness and cleans state (Q72).

Rapid 10Untaggedrapid

Managed vs. external table on drop?

Expanded answer

Managed: data files are deleted. External: files stay (Q93).

Rapid 11Untaggedrapid

Federation vs. ingestion in one sentence?

Expanded answer

Federation queries the source live without copying. Ingestion copies the data in first (Q98).

Rapid 12Untaggedrapid

How do you diagnose skew?

Expanded answer

In the Spark UI, the max task is far bigger than the median in shuffle read or duration (Q12).

Rapid 13Untaggedrapid

What makes a pipeline idempotent?

Expanded answer

A re-run with the same input gives the same output, using MERGE, replace-by-partition or idempotent write IDs (Q61).

Rapid 14Untaggedrapid

What does VACUUM remove?

Expanded answer

Data files no longer referenced and older than the retention window, plus untracked files (Q47).

Rapid 15Untaggedrapid

Why can OPTIMIZE fail to help?

Expanded answer

The filter is not on clustering keys, stats are missing, the slow part is not scanning, or new small files keep arriving (Q48).

Rapid 16Untaggedrapid

Partitioning vs. liquid clustering?

Expanded answer

Partitioning makes folders and is hard to change. Liquid clustering is flexible and can change keys without a rewrite (Q49).

Rapid 17Untaggedrapid

What does mergeSchema do vs. schema enforcement?

Expanded answer

Enforcement rejects unknown columns. mergeSchema lets a write add them (Q52).

Rapid 18Untaggedrapid

Where do duplicates come from in an "exactly-once" stream?

Expanded answer

Duplicate source data, foreachBatch retries, and non-idempotent sinks (Q71).

Rapid 19Untaggedrapid

Directory listing vs. file notification in Auto Loader?

Expanded answer

Listing scans the folder. Notification uses storage events (Q75).

Rapid 20Untaggedrapid

What is the rescued data column?

Expanded answer

A column that holds fields that did not fit the schema, so they are not lost (Q76).

Rapid 21Untaggedrapid

Streaming table vs. materialized view?

Expanded answer

Streaming table: append-only input, each record once. Materialized view: results recomputed to match the current data (Q83).

Rapid 22Untaggedrapid

Expectation actions: warn vs. drop vs. fail?

Expanded answer

Warn keeps bad rows. Drop removes them. Fail stops the update (Q84).

Rapid 23Untaggedrapid

What are the three UC privileges you always need to read a table?

Expanded answer

USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT on the table (Q92).

Rapid 24Untaggedrapid

Why are Python UDFs slow?

Expanded answer

Rows move between the JVM and Python, and Spark cannot optimize them (Q17).

Rapid 25Untaggedrapid

When can caching hurt?

Expanded answer

When I use the data once, or it does not fit in memory (Q18).

Rapid 26Untaggedrapid

What does a Delta commit conflict look like?

Expanded answer

A concurrent modification error at commit time (Q43).

Rapid 27Untaggedrapid

Salesforce SystemModstamp vs. LastModifiedDate?

Expanded answer

SystemModstamp also changes on system updates, so it is the safer cursor (Q128).

Rapid 28Untaggedrapid

How do you handle a 401 vs. a 429 from an API?

Expanded answer

401: refresh the token and retry once. 429: back off and retry (Q129).

Rapid 29Untaggedrapid

What is a deletion vector?

Expanded answer

A side file that marks rows as removed or changed, so Parquet files are not rewritten (Q53).

Rapid 30Untaggedrapid

How do you prove an optimization worked?

Expanded answer

Same data, same compute, cold vs cold, several runs, and a changed plan (Q110).
